category: Quantifiers of small quantity and partial amount

entries.meaning: Marks a small but sufficient number — "some, and enough for the purpose." The speaker is reporting, not complaining. As a pronoun it stands alone with no noun: A few had already left.
examples: I have a few questions before we sign anything.
We stayed a few days longer than we planned.
A few of the seats were still empty when the lights went down.
She knows a few of them from college.
Give it a few minutes and try the link again.
Only a few of the applicants made it past the first round.
entries.русский: несколько — небольшое, но достаточное число исчисляемых; в отличие от few звучит позитивно
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a few chairs, a few minutes, a few people. Never an uncountable noun (✗ a few water, ✗ a few advice) and never a singular countable noun (✗ a few chair).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — a few of the students, a few of my friends, a few of them. Never ✗ a few the students. Before a bare plural noun there is no of: a few students.
entries.pattern: a few [plural countable] · a few of [the/my/these + plural noun] · a few of [them/us/you] · only a few [plural countable] · a few more [plural countable]
entries.contrast: a few is positive, few is negative. A few people came means some came and that was fine; Few people came means almost nobody came and that was a letdown. The countability partner is a little, which does the same positive job for uncountable nouns. And watch quite a few, which contains few but means many — see quite a few.
entries.variants: only a few, just a few, a few more, the few, quite a few (opposite meaning)
entries.see also: few, a little, a couple of, several, one or two, many

entries.meaning: Marks a small but sufficient amount of something uncountable — "some, and enough." As a pronoun it stands alone: I know a little about it.
examples: There's still a little milk left, enough for coffee.
Add a little salt and taste it again.
She speaks a little Portuguese.
It took a little courage to say that out loud.
I've read a little of the report, but not the appendices.
Give me a little more time and I'll have the numbers.
entries.русский: немного — небольшой, но достаточный объём неисчисляемого; позитивно, в отличие от little
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — a little sugar, a little patience, a little time. Never a plural countable noun (✗ a little chairs). It looks as if it takes singular countables in a little dog, but that is a different word: there little is the adjective meaning "small" and a is the ordinary article, which is why a little dog pluralizes to two little dogs while the quantifier cannot (✗ two a little sugars).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — a little of the milk, a little of my time, a little of it. No of before a bare noun: a little milk.
entries.pattern: a little [uncountable noun] · a little of [the/my/this + noun] · a little of [it/that] · just a little [uncountable] · a little more [uncountable]
entries.contrast: a little is positive, little is negative. We have a little time means we are all right; We have little time means we are in trouble. The countability partner is a few. Do not confuse the determiner with the identical adverb a little, which modifies adjectives and verbs rather than nouns (a little tired, rest a little), or with quite a little, which is rare in American English — the American intensifier is quite a bit of.
entries.variants: just a little, only a little, a little more, a little bit of, the little (definite)
entries.see also: little, a few, a bit of, a little bit of, much

examples: Few people showed up, and the ones who did left early.
Few of the proposals survived the first round of cuts.
There are few things I enjoy less than a conference call at seven a.m.
She is one of the few engineers who can read the old firmware.
The few copies still in print sell for hundreds of dollars.
Few, if any, of these results will replicate.

body: Bare few is negative and near-empty: it says the number fell short of what was wanted or expected, and it behaves like a negative in the sentence, taking positive question tags (Few people noticed, did they?) and licensing any (Few of them had any experience). 2. After the, a possessive, or a demonstrative, the negativity drops out and few simply names a small number that does exist — the few options we have left is neutral, even faintly appreciative.
examples: Few people showed up, and the ones who did left early.
Few of the proposals survived the first round of cuts.
There are few things I enjoy less than a conference call at seven a.m.
She is one of the few engineers who can read the old firmware.
The few copies still in print sell for hundreds of dollars.
Few, if any, of these results will replicate.

entries.русский: мало, немногие — только с исчисляемыми; отрицательный оттенок «меньше, чем хотелось бы»
entries.position: central when it opens the noun phrase (few people); postdeterminer after a central determiner (the few people, her few friends, these few days)
entries.register: neutral to formal — in speech Americans usually say not many or hardly any
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — few people, few options. Never an uncountable noun (✗ few time, ✗ few money — use little there) and never a singular countable noun (✗ few option).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — few of the applicants, few of my colleagues, few of them. Never ✗ few the applicants. No of before a bare plural: few applicants.
entries.pattern: few [plural countable] · few of [the/my/these + plural] · [the/her/these] few [plural] · very/so/too few [plural] · few, if any, [plural]
entries.contrast: few vs a few is the central contrast of this file — few is negative ("not many, and that's disappointing"), a few is positive ("some, and that's enough"). The countability partner is little, which is negative in the same way for uncountables: few options but little time. As a determiner it precedes a noun; as a pronoun it stands alone (Few knew what was coming).
entries.variants: very few, so few, too few, precious few, few if any, the few, one of the few
entries.see also: a few, little, fewer, not many, hardly any, precious few / precious little, many

examples: We have little time before the store closes.
There is little evidence that the policy changed anything.
He showed little interest in the offer.
Little of the original building survived the fire.
She spent the little money she had on a bus ticket.
Little did we know that the flight had already been canceled.

body: Bare little is negative: it reports that the amount fell short, and like few it behaves as a negative in the clause, licensing any and taking positive tags (There's little chance, is there?). 2. After the or a possessive it loses the negativity and names the small amount that does exist — the little money he had left is a statement of fact, not a complaint. 3. In the fronted literary frame little did I know, little is an adverb and triggers subject–auxiliary inversion.
examples: We have little time before the store closes.
There is little evidence that the policy changed anything.
He showed little interest in the offer.
Little of the original building survived the fire.
She spent the little money she had on a bus ticket.
Little did we know that the flight had already been canceled.

entries.русский: мало — только с неисчисляемыми; отрицательный оттенок «недостаточно»
entries.position: central when it opens the noun phrase (little time); postdeterminer after a central determiner (the little time we had)
entries.register: neutral to formal; in speech Americans usually say not much or hardly any
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — little time, little evidence, little hope. Never a plural countable noun (✗ little options — use few) and never a singular countable noun in the quantity sense. The adjective little meaning "small" is a different word and does take countable nouns (a little house, those little birds); the giveaway is that the adjective can be graded and compared (littler, the littlest) while the quantifier cannot.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — little of the report, little of my time, little of it. No of before a bare noun: little time.
entries.pattern: little [uncountable noun] · little of [the/my/this + noun] · [the/his] little [uncountable] · very/so/too little [uncountable] · little, if any, [uncountable]
entries.contrast: little vs a little — the article flips the meaning from negative to positive. There is little hope is grim; There is a little hope is not. The countability partner is few: little patience but few options. Also distinguish the adjective (a little dog = a small dog) and the adverb (little did she know, I slept little). As a pronoun little stands alone: Little was said about the cost.
entries.variants: very little, so little, too little, precious little, little if any, little to no, the little
entries.see also: a little, few, less, not much, hardly any, precious few / precious little, scant, much

entries.meaning: Names a smaller number than some other number, stated or implied. As a pronoun it stands alone: Fewer are applying this year.
examples: There were fewer students in the program than the year before.
We need fewer meetings and more time to actually build things.
Fewer of the returning players made the roster this season.
No fewer than twelve agencies had signed off on the plan.
Far fewer people commute downtown now than in 2019.
Each revision left us with fewer and fewer open questions.
entries.русский: меньше (по числу) — сравнительная степень few, только с исчисляемыми
entries.position: central — fewer fills the central determiner slot itself and does not stack under another one: ✗ the fewer errors, ✗ my fewer options, ✗ these fewer meetings. The the of the fewer options we have, the better looks like a counterexample and is not: that the is the adverbial correlative the, not a determiner, which is why the frame needs its second clause to be grammatical at all.
entries.register: neutral; the form careful writing requires
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — fewer errors, fewer cars. Never an uncountable noun (✗ fewer money, ✗ fewer information, ✗ fewer traffic) and never a singular countable noun. This is the one direction of the fewer/less question with no usage debate: fewer simply cannot take a mass noun.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — fewer of the errors, fewer of them. No of before a bare plural: fewer errors.
entries.pattern: fewer [plural countable] · fewer [plural countable] than [phrase/clause] · fewer of [the/these + plural] · no fewer than [number] · far/many/considerably fewer [plural]
entries.contrast: fewer counts, less measures: fewer calories but less fat, fewer employees but less staff. The superlative partner is fewest, and unlike fewer it never takes than. One idiom runs the other way and is fixed: one less thing to worry about is what Americans say, not one fewer thing. And do not confuse fewer with less in the sense "minus" — ten less two is arithmetic, not quantity.
entries.variants: no fewer than, far fewer, fewer and fewer, one fewer, the fewer … the fewer
entries.see also: less, fewest, few, not many, more

entries.meaning: Names the smallest number in a compared set — the superlative of few and fewer. As a pronoun it stands alone: Ours had the fewest.
examples: This route has the fewest traffic lights.
The team with the fewest penalties usually wins the series.
She made the fewest mistakes of anyone in the group.
Pick the option with the fewest moving parts.
Of the three drafts, the last one raised the fewest objections.
We want the fewest possible interruptions during the recording.
entries.русский: наименьшее число — превосходная степень few, только с исчисляемыми
entries.position: postdeterminer — it normally follows the or a possessive (the fewest complaints, our fewest injuries in years); bare fewest occurs mainly in comparative frames (whoever has fewest points)
entries.register: neutral, slightly formal; the least number of and the smallest number of are commoner in speech
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — the fewest errors, the fewest votes. Never an uncountable noun (✗ the fewest money) and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is possible but heavy — the fewest of the complaints is grammatical and rarely said; the natural form attaches fewest directly to a bare plural. Of is required in the partitive pronoun use: the fewest of them.
entries.pattern: the fewest [plural countable] · [possessive] fewest [plural countable] · the fewest of [the/them] · the fewest possible [plural countable]
entries.contrast: fewest counts, least measures: the fewest calories but the least fat. And fewest is a superlative, so it never takes than — that is fewer's job: ✗ fewest errors than last year → ✓ fewer errors than last year. Careful writers who accept less people still tend to keep fewest for counted things, because the least people is odd in a way less people is not.
entries.variants: the fewest possible, the fewest number of (widely criticized as redundant — prefer the smallest number of)
entries.see also: fewer, least, few, most

entries.meaning: Names the smallest amount in a compared set — the superlative of little and less. As a pronoun it stands alone: That's the least I can do.
examples: The plan that causes the least disruption is usually the right one.
Water follows the path of least resistance.
He showed not the least embarrassment about any of it.
Which of these gives us the least exposure to risk?
Losing the deposit was the least of our problems that week.
She wants the least possible attention from the press.
entries.русский: наименьшее количество — превосходная степень little, с неисчисляемыми
entries.position: postdeterminer — it normally follows the (the least trouble); bare least survives in fixed phrases (the path of least resistance, least said, soonest mended)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only in the quantity sense — the least trouble, the least effort, the least resistance. Never a plural countable noun (✗ the least errors — use the fewest) and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — the least of the damage, the least of my worries, the least of them. Most of these are pronoun uses with no following noun.
entries.pattern: the least [uncountable noun] · the least of [my/the + noun] · the least possible [uncountable] · not the least [uncountable] · at least [number/phrase] (adverbial, not a determiner)
entries.contrast: least measures, fewest counts: the least effort but the fewest attempts. Two other leasts are not determiners and should not be confused with this one. The least before an adjective is a superlative degree adverb (the least expensive option, the least likely outcome), the mirror of the most. And at least, not in the least, least of all, and to say the least are fixed adverbial phrases in which least modifies nothing at all.
entries.variants: the least possible, not the least, the very least, least of all, at least (adverbial)
entries.see also: less, fewest, little, most

entries.meaning: Names a smaller amount than some other amount, stated or implied. As a pronoun it stands alone: Less is more.
examples: We're using less electricity since the panels went in.
There was less traffic than I expected for a Friday.
I'd like less salt and more lemon in the dressing.
The trip took less than four hours each way.
She spent less of her own money on it than anyone realized.
That's one less thing to worry about tonight.
entries.русский: меньше (по количеству) — сравнительная степень little, с неисчисляемыми
entries.position: central — less fills the central determiner slot itself and does not stack under another one: ✗ the less noise, ✗ my less time. In the less attention it gets, the better, the the is the adverbial correlative the, not a determiner, so that frame is no exception either.
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — less water, less noise, less enthusiasm. It also goes, in fully standard usage, with plural measures of distance, time, money, weight, and percentage treated as one amount: less than three miles, less than five years, less than $50, less than ten pounds. With ordinary plural countable nouns (less people, less options) it is common in American speech and signage but is corrected to fewer in edited prose. It never takes a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — less of the cake, less of my time, less of it. No of before a bare noun: less cake.
entries.pattern: less [uncountable noun] · less [uncountable] than [phrase/clause] · less of [the/my/this + noun] · no less than [amount] · far/much/considerably less [uncountable] · the less … the less …
entries.contrast: less measures, fewer counts — the rule is real in edited American English but younger than the language, and less has never actually left the plural (see the section note above). Do not confuse the quantifier with the adjective lesser ("smaller in importance": the lesser evil, a lesser charge), with the arithmetic less meaning "minus" (ten less two), or with the conjunctive much less / still less ("let alone": He can't drive, much less fly a plane).
entries.variants: no less than, far less, much less, less and less, one less, nothing less than, couldn't care less
entries.see also: fewer, least, little, not much, more

entries.meaning: Names two, or loosely two or three, of something counted. It is the most everyday small number in American English and is neutral in attitude. As a pronoun it drops both of and the noun and stands alone: I'll take a couple.
examples: Give me a couple of minutes and I'll be ready.
We tried a couple of different approaches before this one worked.
A couple of the reviewers asked for the raw data.
I ran into a couple of them at the airport.
It'll cost a couple of hundred dollars to fix.
Grab a couple chairs from the other room. (informal — of dropped)
entries.pronunciation note: uh KUP-l uhv; in ordinary speech of reduces to /ə/ and the phrase comes out uh KUP-luh
entries.русский: пара, парочка — два, а нестрого два-три; самое обиходное малое число
entries.position: central — the phrase as a whole fills the central determiner slot
entries.register: neutral; the of-less form is informal spoken American
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a couple of days, a couple of people. Never an uncountable noun (✗ a couple of water, ✗ a couple of advice) and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is part of the phrase and is required in writing — a couple of days, a couple of the students, a couple of them. In casual American speech of is routinely dropped before a bare noun (a couple days, a couple times, a couple hundred bucks); this is very common and still nonstandard in edited prose. It is never dropped before a pronoun: ✗ a couple them.
entries.pattern: a couple of [plural countable] · a couple of [the/my/these + plural] · a couple of [them/us] · a couple more [plural] · a couple [plural] (informal, no of)
entries.contrast: a couple of is literally two; a few is roughly three to five. In practice Americans stretch a couple of to "two or three," so it is vaguer than the arithmetic suggests, and a couple of days rarely means exactly forty-eight hours. Against one or two it is slightly more definite; against several it is clearly smaller.
entries.variants: a couple (informal), a couple more, a couple hundred/thousand, the couple of
entries.see also: a few, one or two, several, a handful of, a matter of, dozen

entries.meaning: Names a small number, around five, of counted things — or literally as much as a hand will hold, of an uncountable substance. As a pronoun it drops both of and the noun and stands alone: Only a handful showed up.
examples: Only a handful of people showed up for the vote.
A handful of states have passed similar laws.
She grabbed a handful of rice and threw it at the couple.
A handful of the original team members are still here.
There were a handful of complaints, nothing serious.
I recognized a handful of them from the conference.
entries.русский: горстка — небольшое число, примерно пять
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns in the quantifying sense — a handful of people, a handful of complaints. It also takes uncountable nouns in the literal sense of what fits in a hand — a handful of sand, a handful of rice. Never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory — of is part of the phrase. Before another determiner or pronoun it stays: a handful of the survivors, a handful of them.
entries.pattern: a handful of [plural countable] · a handful of [uncountable, literal] · a handful of [the/these + plural] · a handful of [them] · only a handful of [plural]
entries.contrast: a handful of is roughly five and always carries the flavor of "and that's all" — it leans negative in a way a few does not. A few complaints is neutral; a handful of complaints quietly says the number was small enough not to matter, or in the other direction, small enough to be conspicuous. Verb agreement is normally plural: A handful of students were waiting. Do not confuse the quantifier with the countable noun a handful meaning "someone hard to manage" (that kid is a handful), which takes no of-phrase.
entries.variants: only a handful of, a mere handful of, a handful (pronoun), a fistful of
entries.see also: a couple of, a few, several, a smattering of, a fraction of

entries.meaning: Names a strikingly small span of time, distance, or money — "only this much, and no more."
examples: The building went up in a matter of months.
She missed the record by a matter of inches.
Within a matter of hours the story was everywhere.
It's a matter of dollars, not thousands — just approve it.
The whole outage lasted a matter of minutes.
They were separated by a matter of feet the entire time and never saw each other.
entries.русский: всего каких-нибудь — о поразительно малом сроке, расстоянии или сумме
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns, and almost only units of time, distance, or money — a matter of days, a matter of inches, a matter of dollars, a matter of degrees. It does not take ordinary plural nouns (✗ a matter of students), does not take an uncountable noun in this sense, and takes a singular countable noun only in the unrelated topic sense (a matter of principle).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of is part of the phrase.
entries.pattern: a matter of [plural unit noun] · (only/just) a matter of [plural unit noun] · within a matter of [plural unit noun] · in a matter of [plural unit noun]
entries.contrast: a matter of means "no more than, and strikingly little" — it is only built into a noun phrase, which is why it usually appears after within or in, or with just. The identical-looking a matter of + abstract singular noun is a completely different construction meaning "a question of" (a matter of opinion, a matter of taste, a matter of national security), and as a matter of fact is a fixed adverbial. Against a couple of and a few, this one is the emphatic form: a matter of days dramatizes the shortness in a way a few days does not.
entries.variants: within a matter of, in a matter of, just a matter of, a matter of time (idiom: inevitability)
entries.see also: a couple of, one or two, a few, a fraction of

entries.meaning: Names a vague, moderate quantity of counted things — more than a couple, not enough to specify. It buys the writer precision-free plurality.
examples: A number of issues remain unresolved.
A number of the residents have already filed complaints.
We heard from a number of them after the article ran.
A number of factors contributed to the delay.
A growing number of companies have dropped the requirement.
There are any number of reasons this could have failed.
entries.русский: ряд, некоторое количество — неопределённое умеренное число исчисляемых
entries.register: neutral, faintly formal — common in reports and journalism
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — a number of issues, a number of the delegates. Never an uncountable noun (✗ a number of information — use an amount of) and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of is part of the phrase, and it stays before another determiner or a pronoun: a number of the students, a number of them.
entries.pattern: a number of [plural countable] · a number of [the/these + plural] · a number of [them] · a small/large/growing number of [plural countable]
entries.contrast: the agreement trap is the point of this entry. A number of takes a plural verb; the number of takes a singular verb: A number of issues remain but The number of issues is growing. The indefinite phrase is a quantifier and the plural noun controls agreement; the definite phrase is a real noun phrase headed by number. Note also the countability split with amount: a number of counts, an amount of measures — ✗ a number of water, ✗ an amount of chairs. Bare a number of means roughly "several"; add an adjective and it can go either way (a large number of is a large quantifier).
entries.variants: a small number of, a growing number of, any number of ("a great many"), the number of (different construction)
entries.see also: several, a handful of, a few, many, a large number of

entries.meaning: Names a small part drawn from a larger whole and treated as standing for it — small in size, but chosen rather than merely found.
examples: A sample of 1,200 registered voters was polled last weekend.
The lab ran a sample of the well water for nitrates.
We sent a sample of the fabric to the client before printing the whole run.
A sample of the returning students agreed to be interviewed again.
A random sample of them will be audited each quarter.
The study drew a sample of patients from four hospitals.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/ in ordinary speech, giving uh SAM-pluh
entries.русский: выборка, образец — малая часть, взятая как представитель целого
entries.register: neutral, leaning technical — the ordinary word of survey research, market research, quality control, and the laboratory
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (a sample of voters, a sample of 400 households) and uncountable nouns in the literal, physical sense (a sample of blood, a sample of the soil, a sample of the fabric). Never a singular countable noun in the quantity sense (✗ a sample of respondent). It wants a specified whole behind it: a sample of the population is natural, bare ✗ a sample of population is not.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of is part of the phrase and stays before another determiner or a pronoun: a sample of the students, a sample of them. When the whole is already understood the phrase drops to the bare noun a sample (we took a sample), and that is a noun, not this quantifier.
entries.pattern: a sample of [plural countable] · a sample of [uncountable substance] · a sample of [the/this + noun] · a random/representative sample of [plural countable] · a sample of [number] [plural countable]
entries.contrast: a sample of names a part taken to stand for the whole, and that is what separates it from every other partitive in this section. A handful of voters is merely a few voters; a sample of voters is a few voters chosen to represent all of them. That is why this phrase takes random, representative, stratified, and biased and the others do not. Against a subset of, which claims only membership, a sample of claims representativeness. Verb agreement follows the singular head in careful writing — A sample of 400 voters was surveyed — though plural agreement is common when the writer is thinking of the people rather than of the sample.
entries.variants: a random sample of, a representative sample of, a cross-section of, a subset of, a sample (bare noun)
entries.see also: a subset of, a handful of, a number of, a fraction of, part of

entries.meaning: Names a small number or amount thinly distributed — few, and scattered rather than gathered.
examples: There was a smattering of applause when he finished.
She has a smattering of Italian, enough to order dinner.
A smattering of gray had appeared at his temples.
Only a smattering of tourists come this far north in March.
The lecture assumed a smattering of statistics.
A smattering of early snow was still on the roofs.
entries.русский: крупицы, разрозненные немногие — мало и вразброс, а не в куче
entries.register: neutral to literary
entries.goes with: both plural countable nouns (a smattering of tourists, a smattering of gray hairs, a smattering of complaints) and uncountable nouns — mass nouns such as snow, rain, and applause, and especially the names of languages and fields of knowledge (a smattering of Spanish, a smattering of physics). Never a singular countable noun. Note which side applause falls on: it is uncountable, so a smattering of applause is an uncountable use, and ✗ a smattering of applauses is impossible.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a smattering of [plural countable] · a smattering of [uncountable] · a smattering of [language name] · only a smattering of [noun]
entries.contrast: a smattering of adds scattering to smallness — the items are few and spread thinly, which is why it suits applause, snow, gray hairs, and tourists. Against a handful of, which groups its items, a smattering disperses them. With a subject of knowledge it means superficial acquaintance and carries a mild put-down: a smattering of French means you cannot really speak it, where a little French is neutral.
entries.variants: a sprinkling of, a scattering of, a smattering (pronoun), only a smattering of
entries.see also: a handful of, a trace of, a little, a fraction of

entries.meaning: Names a group whose members all belong to some larger, specified group — the technical register's word for a part of a set.
examples: Only a subset of the users ever open the settings page.
We reran the model on a subset of the data from 2019.
A subset of patients responded to the second-line therapy.
The bug affects a subset of them, mostly on older hardware.
A small subset of the recommendations made it into the final plan.
Every finite set is a subset of itself. (mathematics)
entries.pronunciation note: main stress on SUB; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh SUB-set uh
entries.русский: подмножество, часть — термин: группа внутри большей, названной группы
entries.register: technical — mathematics, statistics, computing, and medicine, plus the corporate prose that borrowed the word from them. It is not a word of ordinary conversation, and some of usually says the same thing more plainly.
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (a subset of users, a subset of the patients) and the mass-like collective nouns of data work (a subset of the data, a subset of the population, a subset of the code). Never a singular countable noun (✗ a subset of user). Like a sample of it wants a specified whole behind it: a subset of the records rather than bare a subset of records.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural, and it takes a definite complement far more often than the other partitives in this file — a subset of the responses, a subset of them.
entries.pattern: a subset of [the + plural countable] · a subset of [the + mass or collective noun] · a small/large subset of [noun] · a subset of [them] · some subset of [noun]
entries.contrast: a subset of says only that the members belong to the larger set; it makes no claim at all about how many there are. A subset of the users may be three people or nearly all of them, which is why the phrase so often needs small or large in front of it before it means anything, and why it sits in this file only loosely. Against a sample of, which is drawn in order to represent the whole, a subset is simply a part of it; against a fraction of, which implies smallness, a subset of implies nothing. In mathematics subset is a strict technical term — every set is a subset of itself — and the office use is a loosened borrowing from it.
entries.variants: a small subset of, some subset of, a proper subset of (mathematics), a segment of, a portion of
entries.see also: a sample of, a number of, a handful of, some, a fraction of

entries.meaning: Names a very small number of counted things, with the vagueness built in on purpose. As a pronoun it stands alone with no noun and takes a plural verb: One or two have already complained.
examples: I have one or two things to finish before I leave.
One or two of the chapters could probably be cut.
There were one or two complaints, but nothing serious.
One or two of them stayed to help clean up.
Just one or two more questions and we're done.
She's made one or two enemies in this building.
entries.русский: один-два — очень малое число, намеренно неточное
entries.register: neutral, conversational
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — one or two things, one or two people. Never an uncountable noun (✗ one or two water) and never a singular countable noun, despite the one — the noun is plural because the phrase as a whole is: One or two things are missing, not ✗ is missing.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — one or two of the chapters, one or two of them. No of before a bare plural: one or two chapters.
entries.pattern: one or two [plural countable] · one or two of [the/these + plural] · one or two of [them/us] · just one or two [plural countable]
entries.contrast: one or two is not arithmetic. It is a deliberate understatement meaning "a small number, and I am not going to be precise about it," and it is regularly used of three or four. Against a couple of it sounds more offhand and more British-inflected but is fully current in American English. Note the reversed twin: [noun] + or two (a day or two, a mile or two, a thing or two), where a thing or two has drifted to mean "quite a lot" and is used sarcastically.
entries.variants: just one or two, a day or two, a thing or two, two or three, a mile or two
entries.see also: a couple of, a few, a handful of, a matter of

entries.meaning: Names a number that is more than two and fewer than many, left deliberately imprecise.
examples: I sent several emails and never heard back.
Several of the students had already dropped the course.
We've been over this several times.
Several hundred people were still without power.
She turned down several of them before accepting this one.
There are several more boxes in the garage.
entries.русский: несколько — больше двух, но не много; нарочито неопределённо
entries.position: central when it opens the noun phrase (several people); postdeterminer after a central determiner in formal use (her several attempts, the several states)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — several emails, several weeks. Never an uncountable noun (✗ several information, ✗ several furniture) and never a singular countable noun (✗ several email).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — several of the students, several of my colleagues, several of them. Never ✗ several the students. No of before a bare plural: several students.
entries.pattern: several [plural countable] · several of [the/my/these + plural] · several of [them/us] · several more [plural countable] · [possessive] several [plural] (formal)
entries.contrast: several sits above a few and below many — roughly three to seven, though the boundaries are soft and nobody counts. It is the most neutral member of the whole section: unlike few it is not disappointed, unlike a handful of it is not dismissive, and unlike a couple of it is not nearly exact. As a determiner it precedes a noun; as a pronoun it stands alone (Several were damaged). Watch the second, unrelated several of formal and legal English meaning "separate, individual" — joint and several liability, the several states — where it is an adjective, not a quantity word.
entries.variants: several more, several other, several hundred/thousand, several times
entries.see also: a few, a handful of, a number of, a couple of, many

examples: There's some coffee left if you want it.
Some of the windows were painted shut.
Would you like some help with those bags?
We spent some time going over the numbers before the call.
Some guy from the leasing office called about the deposit.
I gave some of it away and kept the rest.
Some people never learn.

body: The everyday indefinite quantifier: an unspecified, partial amount or number, neither large nor pointedly small. With an uncountable noun it names part of a mass (some rice); with a plural it names part of a set (some of the seats), and it implies the rest exist — Some of the windows were painted shut invites the question of the others. 2. Before a singular countable noun, stressed /sʌm/, it means "a certain, unidentified, and I don't much care which" — some guy, some excuse or other, some day next week. It is often faintly dismissive. 3. Also stressed, before a singular noun in an exclamation, it is an intensifier of admiration or sarcasm: That was some party. Some help you turned out to be. 4. Before a numeral, some means "approximately" (some twenty people) — that use belongs with the numerals.
examples: There's some coffee left if you want it.
Some of the windows were painted shut.
Would you like some help with those bags?
We spent some time going over the numbers before the call.
Some guy from the leasing office called about the deposit.
I gave some of it away and kept the rest.
Some people never learn.

entries.pronunciation note: the weak /səm/ is the ordinary determiner and is what learners actually hear — some milk comes out [sm̩ ˈmɪlk]; the strong /sʌm/ appears only in the "a certain" and admiring senses below
entries.русский: немного, несколько — неопределённая часть; под ударением перед ед. ч. «какой-то, некий»
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (some chairs) and uncountable nouns (some water) in the quantity sense — this is one of the few quantifiers that takes both. It also takes a singular countable noun, but only in the separate "a certain, unidentified" sense (some guy called); ✗ some chair is impossible as a statement of quantity.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — some of the milk, some of my friends, some of them. Never ✗ some the milk, never ✗ some them. No of before a bare noun: some milk, not ✗ some of milk.
entries.pattern: some [plural countable / uncountable] · some of [the/my/these + noun] · some of [them/it/us] · some [singular countable] ("a certain") · some … others · some more [noun]
entries.contrast: some vs any is the classic pair. Some is the default in affirmative statements (I have some money), any the default in negatives and questions (I don't have any money, Do you have any money?) — and they never combine: ✗ I don't have some money. The rule is a tendency, not a law: some returns in offers and requests, where the speaker expects a yes (Would you like some coffee?, Could I have some water?), and any appears in affirmatives meaning "it doesn't matter which" (Take any seat). Against the rest of this file, some is the neutral baseline — it names a partial amount without judging it, where a few and a little insist the amount is small and few and little complain that it is too small. Determiner some precedes a noun; pronoun some stands alone (Some left early).
entries.variants: some more, some other, some … or other, some few (formal, archaic), somewhat, some + numeral (approximative — a separate use)
entries.see also: any, several, a few, a little, a bit of, some (approximative), a lot of

entries.meaning: Names something that turns up now and then, at irregular intervals — small in frequency rather than in count.
examples: She sends the occasional email, but we haven't really talked in years.
Apart from the occasional thunderstorm, it was a dry summer.
He still makes the occasional spelling mistake, but the writing is clean.
We get the occasional complaint about the noise.
There's the occasional good restaurant along that stretch of highway.
I take the occasional day off in the winter, nothing more than that.
entries.pronunciation note: the takes its pre-vowel form /ði/ here, because occasional begins with the vowel /ə/
entries.русский: редкий, изредка попадающийся — мало по частоте, а не по счёту
entries.position: the fills the central determiner slot and occasional behaves as a postdeterminer inside the frame
entries.register: neutral — the plain American equivalent of British-flavored the odd, and the form to reach for in American writing and speech alike
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns in this frame — the occasional mistake, the occasional email, the occasional late night. Never an uncountable noun in the quantity sense (✗ the occasional traffic). It does combine with plural countable nouns (occasional showers, occasional delays), but that is the plain adjective of frequency doing ordinary adjective work, not this determiner frame, and there it usually appears without the.
entries.with of: Not used — the frame takes no of-phrase. ✗ the occasional of them is impossible; the partitive is built on one: the occasional one of them.
entries.pattern: the occasional [singular countable noun] · [verb] the occasional [singular countable noun] · apart from the occasional [singular countable] · the occasional [singular countable] here and there · occasional [plural countable] (plain adjective, no the)
entries.contrast: the occasional and the odd mean the same thing and fill the same slot; the only difference is register, and the occasional is the one an American writes. Both measure frequency rather than total, which is what separates them from a few: a few emails counts them up, the occasional email spreads them out over time. Both are singular where every other small quantifier of number is plural — the occasional mistake, never ✗ the occasional mistakes in this sense — and that is where learners misfire. Keep the frame apart from the adverb occasionally, which modifies the verb instead (she occasionally emails).
entries.variants: the odd (British-flavored equivalent), the occasional one, occasional (bare adjective with plurals), occasionally (adverb), every so often (adverbial)
entries.see also: the odd, a few, one or two, a smattering of, a handful of

entries.meaning: Names something that happens now and then, infrequently and irregularly — small in frequency rather than in count.
examples: He still makes the odd spelling mistake, but the writing is clean.
We get the odd complaint about the noise.
She'll take the odd day off in the winter.
There's the odd good restaurant out that way.
Apart from the odd thunderstorm, it was a dry summer.
I see him at the odd conference, never anywhere else.
entries.pronunciation note: the takes its pre-vowel form /ði/ here
entries.русский: редкий, время от времени попадающийся — брит. оттенок; амер. эквивалент the occasional
entries.position: the fills the central determiner slot and odd behaves as a postdeterminer inside the frame
entries.register: neutral but distinctly British-flavored; understood everywhere in American English and used mainly in writing with a dry tone. The plain American equivalent is the occasional.
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — the odd mistake, the odd typo, the odd rainy day. Along with the occasional it is one of only two quantifiers in this file that requires a singular noun. Never a plural countable noun (✗ the odd mistakes) and never an uncountable noun (✗ the odd traffic).
entries.with of: Not used — this word takes no of-phrase. ✗ the odd of them is impossible; the partitive is built on one: the odd one of them.
entries.pattern: the odd [singular countable noun] · [verb] the odd [singular countable noun] · the odd [singular countable] here and there
entries.contrast: three different odds sit next to each other and only one is this quantifier. The odd mistake means an occasional mistake, scattered over time. An odd mistake means a strange one. And thirty-odd mistakes means about thirty, where -odd is a suffix on a number. Against a few, this one is about frequency rather than total: a few mistakes counts them up, the odd mistake spreads them out. It is singular where nearly every other quantifier of small number is plural — its one companion in that is the occasional, which means the same thing in plainer American English — and that singular requirement is exactly why learners misfire on it.
entries.variants: the occasional (the everyday American equivalent), the odd one, the odd … here and there, -odd (numeral suffix, different word)
entries.see also: the occasional, a few, one or two, a smattering of, several

entries.meaning: Names a small amount of something uncountable, or with the of a frame, a mild or partial instance of something.
examples: We had a bit of luck with the weather.
Can I give you a bit of advice?
There's still a bit of the cake left in the fridge.
Parking downtown is a bit of a nightmare.
It took a bit of persuading to get her on the plane.
He knows quite a bit of Japanese, actually. (= a lot)
entries.русский: немного, чуть-чуть — малое количество неисчисляемого
entries.register: neutral to informal
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a bit of luck, a bit of trouble, a bit of advice. It reaches singular countable nouns only through the doubled frame a bit of a + noun (a bit of a problem, a bit of a mess), where the second a is obligatory: ✗ a bit of problem. Never a plural countable noun (✗ a bit of chairs).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of is part of the phrase and cannot be dropped: a bit of sugar, a bit of the cake, a bit of it.
entries.pattern: a bit of [uncountable noun] · a bit of [the/my/this + noun] · a bit of a [singular countable noun] · quite a bit of [uncountable] (= a lot) · a bit [adjective] (adverb, not a determiner)
entries.contrast: a bit of and a little are near-synonyms, and the structural difference is of: a little sugar attaches directly to the noun, a bit of sugar cannot. A bit of is the more colloquial of the two and is the one that can take the of a frame. Beware the inversion: quite a bit of means a large amount, the same trap as quite a few. And not a bit means "not at all," which is the negative pole, not a small quantity.
entries.variants: a little bit of, quite a bit of (= a lot), not a bit of, a bit of a, every bit of
entries.see also: a little, a little bit of, a touch of, a couple of

entries.meaning: Names a very small quantity of something soft or spreadable — the amount you would apply with a fingertip or the tip of a knife.
examples: Put a dab of butter on each ear of corn.
It only needs a dab of glue at the corner.
She used a dab of concealer under each eye.
Just a dab of the ointment, twice a day.
He touched up the scratch with a dab of white paint.
Add a dab of mustard and stir it in.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh DAB uh
entries.русский: капелька, мазок — совсем чуть-чуть мягкого или намазывающегося
entries.register: neutral, leaning informal; a domestic, hands-on word at home in kitchens, bathrooms, and workshops
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns naming soft or spreadable substances — a dab of butter, a dab of glue, a dab of paint, a dab of toothpaste, a dab of ointment. Figurative use is rare and stays close to the literal (a dab of color). Never a plural countable noun (✗ a dab of crumbs) and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — ✗ a dab butter.
entries.pattern: a dab of [soft uncountable substance] · just a dab of [uncountable noun] · a dab of [the/this + noun] · put/add a dab of [noun] on [X]
entries.contrast: the small measures divide by the physics of what they measure, and a dab of is the one for something soft that you apply to a surface — butter, glue, cream, paint. A drop of is a liquid that falls, a pinch of a dry powder held between two fingers, and a dollop of a soft substance spooned out, which is distinctly more than a dab. Unlike a bit of and a touch of, this one barely goes figurative at all. Keep it apart from a dab hand at ("someone skilled at"), a British idiom that has nothing to do with quantity.
entries.variants: just a dab of, a smear of, a dollop of (larger), a bit of, a touch of
entries.see also: a dollop of, a drop of, a pinch of, a bit of, a touch of

entries.meaning: Names a very small quantity added to something else — literally in cooking, figuratively of any quality mixed into a whole.
examples: Add a dash of salt and a squeeze of lemon.
The recipe calls for a dash of bitters.
It's a serious book with a dash of humor.
She wanted a dash of color in an otherwise gray room.
Their pitch had ambition and a dash of delusion.
Finish it with a dash of olive oil.
entries.русский: щепотка, капля — чуть-чуть добавленного, в кулинарии и переносно
entries.register: neutral; at home in recipes and in descriptive writing
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — seasonings and liquids literally (a dash of salt, a dash of bitters), and by extension qualities and abstractions (a dash of humor, a dash of color, a dash of skepticism). Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a dash of [uncountable noun] · with a dash of [uncountable noun] · a dash of [the + noun] · [X] with a dash of [Y]
entries.contrast: the culinary smalls divide by what they measure: a dash of for liquids and loose seasonings, a pinch of for dry powders you hold between two fingers, a splash of for a larger pour of liquid, a sprinkling of for something scattered over a surface. All four are freely used figuratively, and in the figurative use a dash of is the flattering one — it names the ingredient that makes the mixture interesting, where a bit of is neutral and a trace of is clinical.
entries.variants: a pinch of (dry), a splash of (liquid), a sprinkling of, a drizzle of, a hint of
entries.see also: a drop of, a pinch of, a hint of, a touch of, a bit of

entries.meaning: Names a soft, rounded spoonful of something — small, but the most generous of the small measures.
examples: Serve the pie warm with a dollop of whipped cream.
Add a dollop of sour cream to each bowl of chili.
She put a dollop of jam in the center of each cookie.
The speech had ambition and a dollop of self-congratulation.
A generous dollop of mashed potatoes went on the plate first.
Stir in a dollop of the yogurt just before serving.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh DAHL-up uh
entries.русский: ложка, шматок — мягкая округлая порция; самая щедрая из «малых» мер
entries.register: neutral; culinary first, and mildly playful when it goes figurative
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns naming soft, semi-solid foods above all — a dollop of sour cream, a dollop of whipped cream, a dollop of jam, a dollop of mashed potatoes — and by extension abstract nouns, usually with a humorous tilt (a dollop of nostalgia, a dollop of self-pity). Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a dollop of [soft uncountable food] · a dollop of [abstract noun] (figurative) · with a dollop of [noun] · a generous dollop of [noun] · a dollop of [the + noun]
entries.contrast: a dollop of is a spoonful — noticeably more than a dab of, more than a dash or a pinch, and unlike all of them it is not apologizing for being small. That is the difference worth learning: most of this section insists the quantity is tiny, while a dollop of names a comfortable, visible serving and readily takes generous or good in front of it. Figuratively it stays warm and slightly comic — a dollop of sentimentality is an affectionate complaint where a trace of sentimentality would be a clinical one.
entries.variants: a generous dollop of, a good dollop of, a spoonful of, a scoop of, a dab of (smaller)
entries.see also: a dab of, a pinch of, a dash of, a bit of

entries.meaning: Names the smallest visible quantity of a liquid, and by extension, under negation, the complete absence of a quality.
examples: Add a drop of vanilla to the batter.
There hasn't been a drop of rain in six weeks.
He showed not a drop of remorse in the interview.
She used every drop of fuel getting back to the airfield.
A drop of blood had dried on the sleeve.
What they're offering is a drop of what it would actually cost.
entries.русский: капля — мельчайшее количество жидкости; при отрицании «ни капли»
entries.register: neutral
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns, chiefly liquids (a drop of water, a drop of blood, a drop of rain) and, under negation, abstract qualities (not a drop of sympathy). Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a drop of [uncountable liquid] · not a drop of [uncountable noun] · every drop of [uncountable noun] · a drop of the [noun]
entries.contrast: a drop of is the smallest of the liquid measures — smaller than a dash of, far smaller than a splash of. Its figurative life is almost entirely negative: not a drop of pity, not a drop of rain all summer. Positively it stays literal, which is what separates it from a hint of and a touch of, both of which are perfectly at home with abstractions in positive sentences. Note the idiom a drop in the bucket, meaning a quantity too small to matter.
entries.variants: not a drop of, every drop of, a drop in the bucket, a splash of, a dash of
entries.see also: a dash of, a trickle of, a trace of, a shred of

entries.meaning: Names a small, faint, but unmistakable amount of an abstract quality — enough to be seen, and usually enough to hope on.
examples: There is a glimmer of hope in this morning's numbers.
She showed not a glimmer of recognition when I said his name.
For the first time in months there was a glimmer of progress.
He answered with a glimmer of the old humor.
The proposal offers a glimmer of relief for renters.
I caught a glimmer of a smile before she turned away.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh GLIM-er uh
entries.русский: проблеск — слабый, но различимый след (надежды, интереса)
entries.register: neutral to literary; common in journalism and in ordinary speech about difficult situations
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns, and a short list of them at that — hope above all, then light, recognition, interest, understanding, doubt, humor. A glimmer of hope accounts for most uses of the phrase in American English. It reaches a singular countable noun only where that noun names an expression or a quality (a glimmer of a smile), and the second article is then required. Never a plural countable noun (✗ a glimmer of options) and never a concrete substance (✗ a glimmer of flour).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural. The literal noun behind the quantifier is an ordinary countable one (a glimmer on the water, the first glimmers of dawn), and that noun takes no of-phrase.
entries.pattern: a glimmer of [abstract noun] · a glimmer of hope (the dominant collocation) · not a glimmer of [abstract noun] · the first glimmer of [abstract noun] · a glimmer of a [singular quality noun]
entries.contrast: a glimmer of names an amount that is faint but visible, and pointed forward — the metaphor is a light that has not gone out yet. That forward tilt separates it from a hint of, which merely registers what is present, and from a trace of, which looks backward at a residue. Unlike a shred of, whose life is almost entirely negative, it works comfortably in positive sentences (there is a glimmer of hope) as well as negative ones (not a glimmer of interest).
entries.variants: a glimmer of hope, not a glimmer of, the first glimmer of, a flicker of, a gleam of, a spark of, a ray of (hope)
entries.see also: a hint of, an inkling of, a trace of, a shred of, a touch of

entries.meaning: Names a barely perceptible amount — enough to notice, not enough to name.
examples: There's a hint of lemon in the sauce.
She answered without a hint of hesitation.
He still has a hint of an accent from somewhere north of Boston.
There was a hint of sarcasm in the reply that everyone caught.
The sky had a hint of pink at the edges.
Not a hint of scandal has ever attached to her name.
entries.русский: намёк, лёгкий оттенок — едва уловимое количество
entries.register: neutral to literary
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns, especially perceptions and qualities registered at the edge of noticing — flavors, smells, sounds, colors, accents, and emotions: a hint of lemon, a hint of an accent, a hint of sarcasm. Never a plural countable noun. It reaches a singular countable noun only where that noun names a quality or feature (a hint of a smile, a hint of an accent), and there the second article is required.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a hint of [uncountable noun] · a hint of a/an [singular quality noun] · without a hint of [uncountable noun] · the merest hint of [noun] · not a hint of [noun]
entries.contrast: a hint of names an amount so small that it is detected rather than measured — the word is about perception, which is why it collocates with senses and moods and sounds wrong with bulk substances (a hint of gravel is odd). Against a touch of, which adds something deliberately, a hint of merely registers it. Against a trace of, which is clinical and often forensic, a hint of is impressionistic. Do not confuse it with the countable noun a hint meaning a clue (give me a hint), which takes no of-phrase in that sense.
entries.variants: the merest hint of, not a hint of, without a hint of, a suggestion of, a whisper of
entries.see also: a touch of, a trace of, a shade of, a dash of

entries.meaning: Names a small amount of something uncountable, with the smallness underlined — the most conversational member of the family.
examples: I need a little bit of help with the last section.
Add a little bit of water if the dough feels dry.
There's a little bit of the old logo still showing through.
It'll take a little bit of time to get used to.
We ran into a little bit of a problem at customs.
Just a little bit of patience and it'll finish installing.
entries.русский: чуть-чуть, самая малость — разг., с подчёркнутой малостью
entries.register: informal to neutral; conversational
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a little bit of sugar, a little bit of help, a little bit of trouble. Like a bit of, it reaches singular countable nouns only through a little bit of a + noun (a little bit of a problem). Never a plural countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of cannot be dropped.
entries.pattern: a little bit of [uncountable noun] · a little bit of [the/my + noun] · a little bit of a [singular countable noun] · just a little bit of [uncountable noun]
entries.contrast: this is the softened, spoken expansion of both a little and a bit of, and the extra words do rhetorical rather than grammatical work — they make the request smaller and the speaker gentler. In writing it is usually trimmed to a little or a bit of. Note that a little bit without of is an adverb, not a determiner: a little bit tired, move over a little bit.
entries.variants: just a little bit of, a little bit (adverb), a wee bit of (jocular), a tiny bit of
entries.see also: a bit of, a little, a touch of

entries.meaning: Names a very small amount of something uncountable — an older, countrified way of saying a bit of.
examples: "We had a mite of trouble with the fence line last spring."
"If he had a mite of sense he'd have stayed home."
The letters gave her a mite of comfort and not much else.
"All we're asking for is a mite of patience, ma'am."
She allowed there had been a mite of talk about it in town.
"It's a mite colder than the radio said." (the surviving adverbial use)
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh MYTE uh
entries.русский: капелька, самая малость — устар. и диал. (южные штаты); наречное a mite живо
entries.register: old-fashioned and rural-flavored. Before a noun (a mite of trouble) it now belongs to older Southern and Midland speech and to fiction reproducing it. What survives nationally is the adverbial a mite — a mite tired, a mite early — which every American recognizes as folksy but current. Read this one; do not write it.
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns, usually abstract and usually naming mild trouble or mild comfort — a mite of trouble, a mite of sense, a mite of comfort, a mite of luck. Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory in the determiner use — ✗ a mite trouble. The of is exactly what separates the determiner from the surviving adverb: a mite of trouble is a quantity, a mite tired is a degree.
entries.pattern: a mite of [abstract uncountable noun] · not a mite of [noun] · a mite [adjective] (adverb, not a determiner) · a mite [comparative] (adverb) · the widow's mite (biblical idiom, a different noun)
entries.contrast: semantically a mite of is simply a bit of, and a bit of is what an American writes today. The word's living home is the adverb — he's a mite slow, that's a mite steep — which is dialect deployed for warmth, the same way nary a is. Keep the quantifier apart from the countable noun mite meaning a tiny arachnid (dust mites) and from the widow's mite, a small coin in the Gospel of Mark.
entries.variants: a mite (adverb: a mite tired), not a mite of, a bit of (the neutral modern equivalent), a tad of, a smidgen of
entries.see also: a bit of, a tad of, a skosh of, a little, a spot of

entries.meaning: Names the minimum decent or acceptable amount of an abstract quality — small, but enough to count.
examples: All we're asking for is a modicum of respect.
The project enjoyed a modicum of success before the funding dried up.
If she had shown even a modicum of remorse, the sentence would have been lighter.
He wants a modicum of privacy, which seems reasonable.
It requires a modicum of skill and a great deal of patience.
Not a modicum of evidence supports that reading.
entries.русский: толика, хоть сколько-нибудь — книжн.: минимум приличного количества
entries.register: formal, often faintly reproachful
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns only — a modicum of respect, a modicum of decency, a modicum of success, a modicum of privacy, a modicum of common sense. It does not take concrete substances (✗ a modicum of water, ✗ a modicum of flour), does not take a plural countable noun, and does not take a singular countable noun. This abstract-only restriction is tighter than that of any other entry in the section.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a modicum of [abstract uncountable noun] · with a modicum of [abstract noun] · not a modicum of [abstract noun] · even a modicum of [abstract noun]
entries.contrast: a modicum of means "at least a minimally acceptable amount," which is why it so often appears in reproach — if he'd shown a modicum of decency implies he showed none. Against a bit of and a little, which are neutral and colloquial, this one is Latinate, formal, and evaluative. Against a shred of, which lives under negation, a modicum of works in positive sentences too (we had a modicum of success).
entries.variants: a measure of, a degree of, some measure of, even a modicum of, a scintilla of (legal)
entries.see also: a shred of, a bit of, a little, minimal

entries.respell: uh PINCH uhv; in ordinary speech the of reduces to /ə/
entries.meaning: Names the smallest cooking measure of a dry ingredient — as much as two fingers will hold — and by extension a very small added amount of anything.
examples: Add a pinch of salt to the flour before you mix it.
The recipe calls for a pinch of saffron, no more than that.
Finish each bowl with a pinch of cinnamon.
It needs a pinch of cayenne, not a spoonful.
Their plan calls for hard work and a pinch of luck.
I used a pinch of the spice mix and saved the rest for later.
entries.pronunciation note: uh PINCH uh salt
entries.русский: щепотка — кулинарная мера сыпучего, и переносно совсем чуть-чуть
entries.register: neutral; the standard small measure of American recipes
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — dry, granular seasonings literally (a pinch of salt, a pinch of saffron, a pinch of cinnamon), and by extension abstract qualities (a pinch of luck, a pinch of skepticism). Never a plural countable noun (✗ a pinch of raisins) and never a singular countable noun (✗ a pinch of onion in the quantity sense).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of is part of the phrase and cannot be dropped: a pinch of salt, a pinch of the spice mix, a pinch of it.
entries.pattern: a pinch of [uncountable noun] · just/only a pinch of [uncountable] · a pinch of [the/this + noun] · add a pinch of [uncountable] · a couple of pinches of [uncountable]
entries.contrast: the culinary smalls divide by what they measure, and a pinch of is the dry one — as much as you can hold between finger and thumb. A dash of is for liquids and loose seasonings, a splash of for a larger pour, a sprinkling of for what is scattered over a surface, and a drop of is smaller than any of them. Figuratively a pinch of is much rarer than a dash of and keeps the flavor of the kitchen when it is used. Two things to keep separate: the noun a pinch meaning a tight spot (in a pinch, feel the pinch), which takes no of-phrase, and the British idiom take it with a pinch of salt — the American form of that idiom is a grain of salt.
entries.variants: just a pinch of, a smidgen of (informal), a dash of (liquid), a sprinkling of, in a pinch (idiom, different sense)
entries.see also: a dash of, a drop of, a touch of, a bit of

entries.meaning: Names the very slightest degree of a quality, most naturally in a negative sentence denying that any exists at all.
examples: There was not a shade of doubt in her voice.
He said it without a shade of irony.
Between the two drafts there isn't a shade of difference.
A shade of regret crossed his face and was gone.
The report contained not a shade of criticism.
It came in a shade under an hour. (adverbial use)
entries.русский: тень, оттенок — малейшая степень качества, чаще при отрицании; неск. устар.
entries.register: literary and slightly dated as a determiner; the adverbial a shade is the living form
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns naming degrees and qualities — a shade of doubt, a shade of irony, not a shade of difference. It does not take a plural countable noun and does not take a concrete substance. In the very common sense "a variety of color," shade of is an ordinary countable noun rather than a quantifier (a shade of blue, three shades of gray), and that use pluralizes freely — which the quantifier does not.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a shade of [abstract uncountable noun] · not a shade of [abstract noun] · without a shade of [abstract noun] · a shade [comparative adjective] (adverb, not a determiner)
entries.contrast: as a determiner a shade of is marginal and mostly survives under negation (not a shade of doubt). What is fully alive in American English is the adverbial a shade before a comparative: a shade too long, a shade better, a shade under an hour. Keep the two apart, and keep both apart from the countable shade of color. Against a hint of, which is current and neutral, a shade of now sounds bookish.
entries.variants: a shade (adverb: a shade too long), not a shade of, shades of (nuances — a different sense), a trace of
entries.see also: a hint of, a trace of, a touch of, slight

entries.meaning: Names a very small amount of something uncountable — the slangiest of the casual American smalls.
examples: Give me a skosh of cream in the coffee, not much.
It needs a skosh of salt and nothing else.
There's a skosh of room left in the trunk.
I'd like a skosh of warning next time.
Add a skosh of water if the dough looks dry.
Scoot over a skosh. (adverbial use, no of)
entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is the one in go; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh SKOHSH uh
entries.русский: чуточку, самую малость — амер. сленг, из японского sukoshi
entries.register: American slang, informal only. It is a borrowing of Japanese sukoshi "a little," carried home by American servicemen stationed in Japan and Korea in the late 1940s and 1950s, and it spread from military slang into general casual speech. Americans meet it in conversation, in cooking talk, and in advertising copy — Levi's sold jeans with "a skosh more room" for years. It does not appear in formal writing.
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a skosh of milk, a skosh of salt, a skosh of patience. Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun. Like a tad, it is used at least as often with no noun at all, as an adverb of degree (a skosh more, a skosh too salty).
entries.with of: obligatory when a noun follows — ✗ a skosh milk. Without of the word is an adverb or a pronoun, not a determiner: a skosh too salty, just a skosh.
entries.pattern: a skosh of [uncountable noun] · just a skosh of [uncountable noun] · a skosh more [noun] (adverbial) · a skosh [comparative adjective] (adverbial) · a skosh (pronoun, standing alone)
entries.contrast: a skosh of, a tad of, and a smidgen of are the three casual American smalls and are freely interchangeable: skosh is the most slangy and the most obviously borrowed, tad the plainest, smidgen the most homespun. All three are near-synonyms of a bit of, which is the neutral form to use in writing. The Japanese origin is worth knowing but is not audible — nothing in skosh signals a loanword to an American ear.
entries.variants: just a skosh of, a skosh (adverb and pronoun), a smidgen of, a tad of, a bit of (neutral)
entries.see also: a tad of, a mite of, a bit of, a little bit of, a touch of

entries.meaning: Names a thin, narrow piece cut or broken from something larger — small in a way you can picture.
examples: She cut herself a sliver of cake and called it dessert.
A sliver of light came in under the door.
There is still a sliver of hope that the bill clears committee.
He pulled a sliver of glass out of his palm.
That program reaches only a sliver of the population that qualifies.
A sliver of moon hung over the parking lot.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh SLIV-er uh
entries.русский: тонкий ломтик, щепка — узкий кусочек, отделённый от большего
entries.register: neutral; at home in food writing, journalism, and physical description
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns for things that can be cut or split thin — a sliver of cheese, a sliver of glass, a sliver of light, a sliver of moon — and abstract nouns in the figurative sense (a sliver of hope, a sliver of doubt, a sliver of the market). With a singular countable noun the second article is required: a sliver of a chance. Never a plural countable noun (✗ a sliver of crackers).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a sliver of [uncountable noun] · a sliver of [abstract noun] (figurative) · a sliver of a [singular countable noun] · the thinnest sliver of [noun] · only a sliver of [noun]
entries.contrast: a sliver of adds shape to smallness: the quantity is small because it is thin and cut from something larger, which is why it suits cake, glass, light, and land, and why it sounds wrong for a powder (✗ a sliver of flour). Against a speck of, which is a dot, a sliver is a line. Against a fraction of, which is arithmetic, a sliver of the market is visual — and that figurative use is a favorite of political and financial writing.
entries.variants: the thinnest sliver of, only a sliver of, a slice of (larger), a shard of (broken rather than cut), a strip of
entries.see also: a speck of, a shred of, a trace of, a bit of, a fraction of

entries.meaning: Names the smallest visible piece of a fine or granular substance — and by extension, nearly always under negation, the total absence of an abstract quality.
examples: There wasn't a speck of dust anywhere in the house.
A speck of something had gotten into my eye.
They found a speck of blood on the doorframe.
He hasn't shown a speck of remorse about any of it.
She wiped up every speck of flour before the inspector came.
There isn't a speck of evidence that the treatment works.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh SPEK uh
entries.русский: крупица, пылинка — мельчайшая частица; почти всегда при отрицании «ни крупицы»
entries.register: neutral; the negative frame not a speck of is much the commonest use in speech
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns naming fine, granular, or particulate matter — a speck of dust, a speck of dirt, a speck of blood, a speck of paint — and, under negation, abstract nouns (not a speck of evidence, not a speck of sympathy). Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural in the quantifier use. The bare countable noun a speck meaning a tiny dot is a different word and takes no of-phrase: a speck on the horizon.
entries.pattern: a speck of [particulate uncountable noun] · not a speck of [noun] · without a speck of [noun] · every speck of [noun] · there isn't a speck of [abstract noun]
entries.contrast: a speck of is the dot among the small measures: the smallest visible piece of something dry or granular, where a drop of is the smallest visible piece of a liquid and a sliver of the smallest cut piece of a solid. Its figurative life is almost entirely negative and emphatic (not a speck of proof), which puts it beside a shred of rather than beside a hint of. Note that not a speck of dust is a compliment about housekeeping, not a complaint.
entries.variants: not a speck of, every speck of, a fleck of, a grain of, a particle of, a speck (countable noun)
entries.see also: a sliver of, a drop of, a trace of, a shred of, a pinch of

entries.meaning: Names a small amount of something uncountable — a British quantifier that American English keeps only for effect.
examples: We ran into a spot of trouble at the border.
Fancy a spot of lunch?
There's a spot of rain forecast for the afternoon.
He's had a spot of bother with the neighbors.
She stopped for a spot of tea and stayed two hours.
After a spot of difficulty with the visa, everything went smoothly.
entries.русский: немножко — брит.: a spot of tea, a spot of trouble; в амер. англ. шутливо
entries.register: chiefly British. In American English it survives in a narrow band of set phrases — a spot of trouble, a spot of bother, a spot of tea, a spot of lunch — and almost always with a deliberately arch or jocular British flavor. It is not neutral American usage, and a learner should recognize it rather than reach for it.
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a spot of trouble, a spot of rain, a spot of tea. Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a spot of [uncountable noun] · a spot of [trouble/bother/lunch/tea] · a spot of [the + noun]
entries.contrast: semantically a spot of is just a bit of, and that is the substitution an American writer should make: a bit of trouble, not a spot of trouble, unless the British register is the point. Note the separate literal noun a spot of meaning a small mark of something (a spot of grease on the tie), which is not this quantifier and is perfectly ordinary in American English.
entries.variants: a bit of (the neutral American equivalent), a spot of bother (British idiom), a touch of
entries.see also: a bit of, a touch of, a little

entries.meaning: Names a very small amount of something uncountable — the plainest of the casual American smalls, and frequently an understatement.
examples: Add a tad of honey if it's too tart.
I'd like a tad of milk in mine.
It'll take a tad of patience to get through the phone tree.
There's a tad of room left on the drive, not much.
We had a tad of trouble finding the entrance.
The rent is a tad steep for that neighborhood. (adverbial use, no of)
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh TAD uh
entries.русский: чуточку — разг. амер., часто как преуменьшение
entries.register: informal, thoroughly American and thoroughly current in speech; rare in edited writing, which trades it for a little or slightly
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — a tad of salt, a tad of luck, a tad of patience. Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun. Note that the of-less uses are far commoner than this determiner one: a tad is heard mostly as an adverb of degree (a tad late, a tad expensive, a tad too sweet) or as a bare pronoun (just a tad).
entries.with of: obligatory whenever a noun follows — ✗ a tad salt. Drop the of and the word stops being a determiner: a tad of sugar is a quantity, a tad sweet is a degree, and only the first belongs in this file.
entries.pattern: a tad of [uncountable noun] · just a tad of [uncountable noun] · a tad [adjective] (adverb, not a determiner) · a tad more [noun] (adverbial) · a tad (pronoun, standing alone)
entries.contrast: a tad of is the everyday casual equivalent of a bit of, and among the informal smalls it is the one an American is likeliest to say — plainer than a skosh of, less countrified than a mite of, less twee than a smidgen of. Its most characteristic use is not quantitative at all but the understating adverb: a tad expensive usually means "outrageously expensive," said dryly.
entries.variants: just a tad of, a tad (adverb and pronoun), a tad more, a smidgen of, a skosh of, a bit of (neutral)
entries.see also: a skosh of, a mite of, a bit of, a touch of, a little bit of

entries.meaning: Names a small amount added to or present in something — enough to change the character of the whole without dominating it.
examples: Add a touch of garlic, but don't overdo it.
He's got a touch of gray at the temples now.
She's been out with a touch of the flu.
The room needed a touch of color.
There was a touch of frost on the windshield this morning.
The whole production had a touch of class about it.
entries.русский: нотка, лёгкая примесь — немного, но достаточно, чтобы изменить оттенок целого
entries.register: neutral; thoroughly at home in American English
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — flavors, colors, qualities, and mild illnesses: a touch of garlic, a touch of gray, a touch of class, a touch of frost. Never a plural countable noun and never a singular countable noun in the quantity sense. With illnesses it takes an idiosyncratic definite article: a touch of the flu, a touch of the blues — an unusual double determiner licensed only by this frame.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a touch of [uncountable noun] · a touch of the [illness] · with a touch of [uncountable noun] · a touch [adjective] (adverb, not a determiner)
entries.contrast: a touch of adds something on purpose — a cook adds a touch of garlic, a designer adds a touch of color.
