That intentionality is what separates it from a hint of, which only registers what is there, and from a trace of, which is forensic. It is the natural American alternative to British a spot of. And a touch without of is an adverb of degree: a touch salty, a touch early.
entries.variants: a touch (adverb), just a touch of, a touch of the (illnesses), a hint of, a dash of
entries.see also: a hint of, a dash of, a bit of, a spot of

entries.meaning: Names the smallest detectable amount of something — the amount an instrument, or a careful observer, can just barely find.
examples: The lab found a trace of lead in the water.
There was a trace of an accent, but I couldn't place it.
The plane vanished without a trace of wreckage.
Not a trace of the original paint has survived.
She answered with a trace of impatience.
The supplement contains trace amounts of iodine. (attributive)
entries.русский: след, следы — мельчайшее обнаружимое количество; тех. и криминалистическое
entries.register: neutral, leaning technical and forensic
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — substances detected in tiny quantities (a trace of arsenic, a trace of moisture) and abstract qualities (a trace of an accent, a trace of bitterness). Never a plural countable noun. It reaches a singular countable noun only where that noun names a quality or a residue (a trace of a smile, a trace of an accent), and the second article is then required.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural. Note the article-less attributive form trace amounts of, trace elements, trace minerals, where trace has become an adjective.
entries.pattern: a trace of [uncountable noun] · no trace of [noun] · without a trace of [noun] · trace amounts of [noun] (attributive) · not a trace of [noun]
entries.contrast: a trace of is the vocabulary of detection: it means the smallest amount an instrument or an observer can find, which is why it dominates lab reports, toxicology, and police procedurals. The negative no trace of is far commoner than the positive, and vanish without a trace is fixed. Against a hint of, which is impressionistic, a trace of claims to be measured; against a shred of, which is only ever abstract and only ever negated, a trace of takes concrete substances and works in positive sentences.
entries.variants: no trace of, without a trace, trace amounts of, trace elements, not a trace of, the faintest trace of
entries.see also: a hint of, a shred of, a drop of, a smattering of

entries.meaning: Names a small quantity arriving or moving slowly and continuously — small in rate rather than in bulk.
examples: There was only a trickle of water coming from the tap.
Applications slowed to a trickle of two or three a week.
We're getting a trickle of information out of the agency.
A steady trickle of visitors kept the museum open.
Funding has been reduced to a trickle of what it once was.
A trickle of blood had dried along his jaw.
entries.русский: тонкая струйка — мало по темпу поступления, а не по объёму
entries.register: neutral; common in journalism
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns literally (a trickle of water, a trickle of blood) and, figuratively, plural countable nouns regarded as a slow stream (a trickle of applicants, a trickle of visitors) and abstract mass nouns (a trickle of information, a trickle of funding). Never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: a trickle of [uncountable noun] · a trickle of [plural countable, figurative] · down to a trickle of [noun] · a steady trickle of [noun]
entries.contrast: a trickle of adds slowness over time to smallness — the quantity is small because it arrives gradually, not because there is little of it in total. That is what separates it from a bit of and a drop of, which are static. Its opposites are the large-quantity flow words: a stream of, a flood of, a torrent of, a deluge of. Verb agreement follows the singular head in careful writing — A trickle of visitors was still arriving — though plural agreement is common in speech when the noun after of is plural.
entries.variants: a steady trickle of, down to a trickle, a trickle (pronoun), a stream of (larger), a flood of (opposite)
entries.see also: a drop of, a smattering of, a fraction of, a handful of

entries.meaning: Names an unspecified but real amount of an abstract quality present in a situation — "some of this is in play, and I am not going to say how much."
examples: There is an element of truth in what he said, but only an element.
Every one of these trades carries an element of risk.
The plan depended entirely on an element of surprise.
Her account leaves an element of doubt that the report never addresses.
There was an element of luck in the way the schedule fell.
The job has an element of danger that the posting never mentioned.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ən/, never /æn/, and the of reduces to /ə/, giving uhn EL-uh-munt uh
entries.русский: доля, элемент — некоторая, намеренно не уточняемая примесь качества
entries.register: neutral to formal — common in journalism, analysis, legal writing, and careful speech
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns — an element of truth, an element of risk, an element of surprise, an element of doubt, an element of luck, an element of danger. Never a plural countable noun, and never a concrete substance in the quantity sense (✗ an element of water — that is the chemistry noun). It reaches a singular countable noun only where the noun is itself abstract (an element of a defense), and the second article is then required.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural. Note that the article is an rather than a because element begins with a vowel — the same adjustment an inkling of and an iota of make.
entries.pattern: an element of [abstract uncountable noun] · there is an element of [noun] in [X] · not without an element of [noun] · a strong/large element of [noun] · the element of surprise (fixed, definite)
entries.contrast: an element of concedes rather than measures. There is an element of truth in that grants that some truth is present while declining to say how much, and the concession is usually the front half of a sentence whose second half begins with but. That argumentative job is what separates it from a hint of, which is about perception, and from a modicum of, which is about sufficiency. Keep the quantifier apart from the ordinary countable noun element meaning a component or a chemical substance (the elements of a contract, seventeen elements), which pluralizes freely where the quantifier cannot.
entries.variants: the element of surprise, a large element of, some element of, an aspect of, a degree of, a measure of
entries.see also: a modicum of, a hint of, a glimmer of, a trace of, some

entries.meaning: Names the faintest amount of awareness or suspicion — just enough knowledge to register that something is there.
examples: She had an inkling of what the meeting was really about.
Nobody had an inkling of trouble until the second quarter.
He gave us an inkling of the direction the company was heading.
I hadn't the faintest inkling of how expensive it would be.
There was an inkling of suspicion in the way she asked.
If they'd had an inkling of the cost, they would never have started.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ən/; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uhn INK-ling uh
entries.русский: смутная догадка, малейшее подозрение — едва-едва осознавать, что что-то есть
entries.register: neutral, slightly literary; commonest in narrative and in reports of what somebody did or did not know
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns of knowledge and awareness, and a narrow set at that — an inkling of trouble, an inkling of the truth, an inkling of suspicion. Very often it takes a clause instead of a noun: an inkling of what he meant, an inkling of how bad it was. Never a plural countable noun and never a concrete substance.
entries.with of: obligatory before a noun or a wh-clause. With a that-clause the of disappears: I had an inkling that she'd say no, never ✗ an inkling of that she'd say no. The bare noun also stands alone: I hadn't the faintest inkling.
entries.pattern: an inkling of [abstract noun] · an inkling of [what- or how-clause] · an inkling that [clause] · not the faintest inkling of [noun] · have/get/give someone an inkling of [noun]
entries.contrast: an inkling of measures knowledge, not substance — it is the smallest amount of awareness a person can have of something, which is why it collocates with have, get, and give and leans hard on negation (no inkling, not the faintest inkling). That is what separates it from a hint of, which is a property of the thing rather than of the knower: a remark can carry a hint of sarcasm, but only a person can have an inkling of it. Against a glimmer of, which looks forward hopefully, an inkling is neutral and often uneasy.
entries.variants: not the faintest inkling of, no inkling of, an inkling that, an inkling (bare noun), a suspicion of, a hint of
entries.see also: a glimmer of, a hint of, an element of, a trace of, a shred of

entries.meaning: Names an amount or number that falls short of what the situation requires — a scarcity, stated with disapproval.
examples: There is a dearth of affordable housing in every county in the state.
The investigation was hampered by a dearth of physical evidence.
A dearth of qualified applicants has kept three positions open since May.
The literature shows a paucity of long-term follow-up data. (the academic equivalent)
What the report reveals is a dearth of imagination, not a dearth of money.
After a decade of a dearth of new construction, permits are finally rising.
entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is the one in bird, not the one in dear; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh DURTH uh
entries.русский: нехватка, дефицит — книжн.: меньше, чем требуется, с оттенком осуждения
entries.register: formal to journalistic — a leader-column word. Its close synonym a paucity of is a step more formal again and belongs to academic and technical prose (a paucity of data, a paucity of evidence), where a dearth of is what an editorial writer reaches for.
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (a dearth of information, a dearth of evidence, a dearth of talent, a dearth of funding) and plural countable nouns (a dearth of options, a dearth of qualified applicants). It is one of the few phrases in this file that takes both noun types with no change of meaning. Never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural — of is part of the phrase and stays before another determiner (a dearth of the skills we need), though pronoun complements are rare and awkward.
entries.pattern: a dearth of [uncountable noun] · a dearth of [plural countable noun] · there is a dearth of [noun] · a relative dearth of [noun] · a paucity of [noun] (the academic equivalent)
entries.contrast: a dearth of does not merely report that an amount is small; it says the amount is too small. It is a complaint dressed as a measurement, and it presupposes a standard that has not been met. That evaluative charge separates it from a shortage of, which is practical and temporary, and from a lack of, which is blunter, far commoner, and states plain absence rather than insufficiency. A dearth of also carries a faint mustiness, and a plain writer is often better served by not enough.
entries.variants: a paucity of (academic), a shortage of, a scarcity of, a relative dearth of, a lack of, a want of (archaic)
entries.see also: a lack of, a want of, scant, precious few / precious little, little

entries.meaning: Names the smallest imaginable amount of an abstract quality, used only to deny that even that much is present — the King James Bible's minimizer.
examples: "Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law." (Matthew 5:18)
He would not yield a jot of the ground he had taken.
There is not a jot of evidence in the whole of the correspondence.
"It does not signify a jot of difference to me which of them wins."
She never abated a jot of her conviction that the letters were forged.
Nothing the witness said altered the case a jot. (bare adverbial use)
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh JAHT uh
entries.русский: ни на йоту — устар., библейск.: мельчайшая доля, только при отрицании
entries.register: archaic and literary. The word is iota, the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, worn down in transmission, and it entered English on the King James rendering of Matthew 5:18 — "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law." An American meets it in scripture, in nineteenth-century prose, and in writing deliberately reaching for that sound. Nobody says it at the lunch counter. The everyday verb jot down is a different word entirely in feel.
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns — a jot of evidence, a jot of sense, a jot of difference, a jot of sympathy. Never a plural countable noun and never a concrete substance. It is used at least as often with no of-phrase at all: not a jot, not one jot.
entries.with of: required when a noun follows (✗ a jot evidence), but the phrase very often stops at the bare noun and works adverbially — it does not matter a jot.
entries.pattern: not a jot of [abstract noun] · without a jot of [abstract noun] · not a jot (bare adverbial) · not one jot · jot or tittle (the biblical doublet)
entries.contrast: a jot of and a whit of are the two archaic minimizers of English and they are interchangeable — jot comes from Greek iota, whit from Old English wiht "creature, thing." Both do the work that a shred of and an iota of do in living American English, and either of those is what a writer should use today. Like all of them it is negative-polarity: it needs a negation, and a plain affirmative ✗ We have a jot of evidence is impossible.
entries.variants: not a jot, not one jot, jot or tittle, a whit of, an iota of (the modern form), a shred of
entries.see also: a whit of, an iota of, a shred of, a scintilla of

entries.meaning: Names the absence of something, or an amount of it too small to serve — the ordinary, unmarked way of saying there is not enough.
examples: The case was thrown out for a lack of evidence.
A lack of sleep is showing in everybody by Thursday.
What killed the project was a lack of funding, not a lack of interest.
There is a lack of affordable options for families in this district.
For lack of a better word, the whole afternoon was a mess.
His answer showed a complete lack of interest in the details.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh LAK uh
entries.русский: отсутствие, нехватка — обычный, нейтральный способ сказать «недостаточно»
entries.register: neutral — much the commonest of the shortage phrases, and equally at home in speech, journalism, and formal writing
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (a lack of evidence, a lack of sleep, a lack of interest, a lack of funding) and plural countable nouns (a lack of options, a lack of qualified teachers). It also takes a singular countable noun where that noun is abstract enough to be treated as a quality — a lack of a plan, a lack of a clear answer — and there the second article is required.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural. Note the article-free frame for lack of (for lack of a better word, dismissed for lack of evidence), which is fixed and very common, and the article-free lack of of headlines and captions.
entries.pattern: a lack of [uncountable noun] · a lack of [plural countable noun] · for lack of [noun] (no article) · a complete/total lack of [noun] · due to a lack of [noun]
entries.contrast: a lack of states plain absence or insufficiency and does not editorialize, which is exactly what separates it from a dearth of, which complains, and from a shortage of, which implies a supply that ought to be replenished. It is the phrase to reach for when the others sound overdressed. Two cautions. It heads a singular noun phrase and takes a singular verb — A lack of resources was the problem, not ✗ were the problem. And it is already negative, so a second negation reverses the sense: a lack of progress means no progress, and ✗ a lack of no evidence says the opposite of what is meant.
entries.variants: for lack of, a complete lack of, a total lack of, lack of (headline style), an absence of, a shortage of
entries.see also: a dearth of, a want of, next to no, hardly any, little

entries.meaning: Names the smallest conceivable amount of evidence or support — a spark of it — used to deny that even that much exists, or in law to state the minimum a party must show.
examples: There is not a scintilla of evidence connecting my client to the vehicle.
The plaintiff must produce more than a scintilla of evidence to survive summary judgment.
The panel found not a scintilla of support for that reading of the statute.
He made the accusation without a scintilla of proof.
The record does not contain a scintilla of evidence of discriminatory intent.
Not a scintilla of doubt was raised at trial about the chain of custody.
entries.pronunciation note: stress on the second syllable; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh sin-TIL-uh uh
entries.русский: юр.: мельчайшая доля, «искра» — о минимуме доказательств; вне суда не употребляется
entries.register: legal. Latin scintilla means "spark." In American law the phrase is a term of art: the scintilla rule and the "more than a scintilla of evidence" threshold recur constantly in summary-judgment and directed-verdict opinions, where a party opposing judgment must produce more than a scintilla of evidence to reach a jury. Outside a courtroom, a brief, or a law review an American meets it only when a writer is borrowing the courtroom's voice on purpose. It is not ordinary English and should not be written as though it were.
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns, and a very short list of them — evidence above all, then proof, support, doubt, merit. Never a plural countable noun, never a singular countable noun, and never a concrete substance (✗ a scintilla of water).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: not a scintilla of [abstract noun] · more than a scintilla of [evidence] (the legal threshold) · without a scintilla of [noun] · there is not a scintilla of [noun] · no scintilla of [noun]
entries.contrast: a scintilla of is the courtroom's a shred of, and in bare meaning the two are interchangeable. What differs is that scintilla drags a legal test behind it: "more than a scintilla" is a bar a party has to clear, which is why this phrase — alone among the emphatic minimizers — appears freely in the affirmative (the record contains more than a scintilla of evidence) even though ordinary use is negative. Against an iota of, the everyday emphatic minimizer, a scintilla of is the one that will sound like a lawyer talking.
entries.variants: not a scintilla of, more than a scintilla of (the legal threshold), no scintilla of, a shred of, an iota of, a particle of
entries.see also: a shred of, an iota of, a jot of, a whit of, de minimis

entries.meaning: Names the smallest conceivable amount of an abstract quality, used almost always to deny that even that much exists.
examples: There isn't a shred of evidence for any of this.
He left without a shred of dignity.
She hasn't shown a shred of remorse.
Not a shred of doubt remained after the second test.
The story has no shred of credibility.
They didn't have an ounce of proof, and they filed anyway.
entries.русский: ни капли, ни грамма — мельчайшая доля качества, почти всегда при отрицании
entries.register: neutral to formal; emphatic
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns only — evidence, proof, doubt, dignity, decency, remorse, self-respect, credibility. Never a plural countable noun, never a singular countable noun, and not a concrete substance in this sense (a shred of paper is the literal noun, not the quantifier).
entries.with of: obligatory and structural.
entries.pattern: not a shred of [abstract noun] · without a shred of [abstract noun] · there isn't a shred of [abstract noun] · no shred of [abstract noun]
entries.contrast: a shred of is almost exclusively negative-polarity: it needs a negative, and a bare positive We have a shred of evidence sounds wrong. This is what separates it from a modicum of, which works in positive sentences. It has a family of interchangeable emphatic partners — an ounce of, an iota of, a scrap of, a particle of, and in legal writing a scintilla of — plus two that are locked to a single noun each: a lick of work and a stitch of clothing. The older a whit of and a jot of are archaic and read as deliberately literary.
entries.variants: an ounce of, an iota of, a scrap of, a particle of, a scintilla of (legal), a lick of (work), a stitch of (clothing), a whit of (archaic), a jot of (archaic)
entries.see also: an iota of, a scintilla of, a modicum of, a trace of, not much, hardly any

entries.meaning: Names an absence or insufficiency of something — the older word that a lack of has very nearly replaced.
examples: For want of a nail the shoe was lost; for want of a shoe the horse was lost.
The appeal was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
He agreed to it for want of anything better to do that evening.
"The house was cold and cheerless, for want of a fire and for want of company."
It failed for want of capital, not for want of ideas.
Call it a truce, for want of a better word.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh WAHNT uh
entries.русский: нехватка, отсутствие — устар. и юр.; современный вариант — a lack of
entries.register: archaic and formal. In current American English it survives almost entirely inside fixed frames — for want of a better word, for want of anything better to do, and the proverb for want of a nail the shoe was lost — plus legal boilerplate, where dismissed for want of prosecution and for want of jurisdiction are live phrases on court dockets today. Free use before an ordinary noun (a want of evidence) reads as nineteenth-century prose. The modern everyday form is a lack of.
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns (a want of evidence, a want of sense, a want of charity, a want of prosecution) and, in older prose, plural countable nouns (a want of hands, a want of provisions). Never a singular countable noun except inside the for want of a frame, where the second article is required: for want of a nail.
entries.with of: obligatory and structural. The dominant surviving form drops the article altogether: for want of [noun], not ✗ for a want of [noun].
entries.pattern: for want of [noun] (the living frame) · for want of a [singular countable noun] · a want of [abstract uncountable noun] (archaic) · dismissed for want of [prosecution/jurisdiction] (legal) · from want of [noun]
entries.contrast: a want of and a lack of mean the same thing, and a lack of has taken over everywhere except the fixed phrases — for want of a better word and for lack of a better word are both idiomatic, but a want of evidence should become a lack of evidence in anything written today. Against a dearth of, which is formal but current, a want of is formal and dated. Keep it apart from the ordinary verb want and from the countable noun a want meaning a desire (his wants are few).
entries.variants: for want of, for want of a better word, for want of anything better, for want of prosecution (legal), a lack of (the modern equivalent)
entries.see also: a lack of, a dearth of, a jot of, a whit of, next to no

entries.ipa: /ə ˈwɪt əv/, with the older wh- kept in some regional speech /ə ˈʍɪt əv/
entries.meaning: Names the smallest conceivable amount of an abstract quality, used only to deny it — an old word kept alive by old books.
examples: "He cared not a whit for what the neighbors might say."
There is not a whit of evidence in the record to support the charge.
The revision made not a whit of difference to the outcome.
"She abated not a whit of her demands."
Twenty years in office had not softened him a whit.
They showed not a whit of remorse when the verdict came down.
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of wit for most Americans; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uh WIT uh
entries.русский: ни на йоту, ни капли — устар., книжн., только при отрицании
entries.register: archaic and literary. From Old English wiht, "creature, thing." It belongs to older prose and to modern writing imitating it, and its commonest surviving shape is the bare adverbial not a whit, meaning "not at all" — he cared not a whit. Americans read this phrase; they do not say it.
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns — a whit of evidence, a whit of sense, a whit of difference, a whit of sympathy. Never a plural countable noun and never a concrete substance.
entries.with of: required when a noun follows, but the phrase very often stops at the bare noun and works adverbially: not a whit, never a whit, cared not a whit.
entries.pattern: not a whit of [abstract noun] · without a whit of [abstract noun] · not a whit (bare adverbial) · care/matter not a whit · never a whit
entries.contrast: a whit of is the twin of a jot of — same job, same era, different ancestry — and both are archaic where a shred of and an iota of are current. Like them it is negative-polarity and cannot stand in a plain affirmative: ✗ We found a whit of evidence. Note how close not a whit is to not a bit: the second is ordinary modern English, the first is costume.
entries.variants: not a whit, never a whit, a jot of, an iota of (the modern form), not a bit (the modern adverbial)
entries.see also: a jot of, an iota of, a shred of, a scintilla of

entries.meaning: Names the smallest conceivable amount of an abstract quality, used almost always to deny that any of it exists at all.
examples: There isn't an iota of evidence that he knew about the transfer.
She hasn't shown an iota of remorse.
Not one iota of the plan has changed since March.
The apology contained not an iota of sincerity.
It won't make an iota of difference who signs it.
He answered without a particle of embarrassment. (the literary variant)
entries.pronunciation note: the article is the weak /ən/; the of reduces to /ə/, giving uhn eye-OH-tuh uh
entries.русский: ни капли, ни на йоту — мельчайшая доля; живой эмфатический оборот
entries.register: neutral to formal, emphatic — a live American phrase. It is named for iota, the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, but the etymology is invisible in use, and it should not be confused on that account with a jot of, which descends from the same Greek word and is archaic. Its rarer partner a particle of does identical work with a bookish air.
entries.goes with: uncountable abstract nouns — evidence, proof, doubt, sense, sympathy, credibility, difference, remorse. Never a plural countable noun, never a singular countable noun, and never a concrete substance (✗ an iota of sugar).
entries.with of: obligatory when a noun follows. The bare noun also stands alone adverbially: it doesn't matter an iota, not one iota.
entries.pattern: not an iota of [abstract noun] · without an iota of [abstract noun] · there isn't an iota of [abstract noun] · not one iota (bare, emphatic) · not an iota [comparative]
entries.contrast: an iota of is negative-polarity: it needs a negation, and a plain affirmative ✗ We have an iota of evidence is not English. It belongs to the emphatic family headed by a shred of, alongside an ounce of, a scrap of, a particle of, and a speck of; of these it is the most abstract and the most emphatic, and it is the one that pairs with one for extra force (not one iota). Against a scintilla of, a legal term of art, an iota of is plain English; against a jot of and a whit of, which are archaic, it is fully current.
entries.variants: not one iota, not an iota, a particle of (literary), an ounce of, a scrap of, a shred of, a scintilla of (legal)
entries.see also: a shred of, a scintilla of, a jot of, a whit of, a speck of, a modicum of

entries.meaning: Names a quantity so small it is on the edge of nothing — "almost none, but not quite none."
examples: There's barely any milk left.
Barely any of the seats were taken.
We had barely any warning before the road closed.
Barely any of them showed up for the second session.
She's had barely any sleep this week.
There was barely any difference between the two versions.
entries.русский: почти нисколько — количество на грани нуля, но не совсем ноль (разг.)
entries.position: barely modifies the central determiner any, which fills the central slot
entries.register: neutral to informal — the most colloquial of the three any phrases
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (barely any people) and uncountable nouns (barely any time). Never a singular countable noun (✗ barely any chair).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — barely any of the seats, barely any of it. No of before a bare noun: barely any seats.
entries.pattern: barely any [plural countable / uncountable] · barely any of [the/my/these + noun] · barely any of [them/it] · there's barely any [noun] · barely any (pronoun, standing alone)
entries.contrast: barely any, hardly any, and scarcely any are near-interchangeable and differ mainly in register: barely is the most casual, hardly the everyday default, scarcely the most formal. All three are negative-polarity and keep the verb positive: ✓ There's barely any left / ✗ There isn't barely any left, which is negative concord and nonstandard in writing. Against bare few and little, these are what Americans actually say.
entries.variants: hardly any, scarcely any, barely anything (pronoun), barely a (+ singular noun)
entries.see also: hardly any, scarcely any, next to no, not much, little

entries.meaning: Names a number that is small and may in fact be zero — a hedge that intensifies rather than softens.
examples: Few, if any, of the proposals will survive committee.
Few, if any, American cities have solved this.
There are few, if any, precedents for a ruling like that.
Few, if any, of them had read the contract.
The drug produced few, if any, measurable benefits.
Few, if any, of the original documents remain.
entries.русский: мало, если вообще есть — оговорка, которая усиливает, а не смягчает
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in journalism, academic prose, and argument
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — few if any survivors, few if any of the proposals. Never an uncountable noun — the uncountable partner is little if any (little if any evidence). Never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — few if any of the applicants, few if any of them. No of before a bare plural: few if any applicants.
entries.pattern: few, if any, [plural countable] · few, if any, of [the/these + plural] · [noun phrase] — few, if any — [verb] · little, if any, [uncountable] (the uncountable partner)
entries.contrast: the commas matter: in edited prose it is normally punctuated few, if any, as a parenthetical, and dropping them (few if any proposals) reads as more casual. Against bare few, this frame is emphatic — it concedes that the true number may be zero, which is a stronger claim than few alone. Its uncountable twin is little if any, and its blunter cousins are few or none and little to no.
entries.variants: little if any (uncountable), few or none, little or none, if any (standing alone)
entries.see also: few, precious few / precious little, next to no, hardly any

entries.meaning: Names a quantity or number so small as to be nearly none — the ordinary spoken replacement for few and little.
examples: There's hardly any time before the flight.
Hardly any of the students finished the exam.
We got hardly any snow this winter.
Hardly any of them stayed for the second half.
She has hardly any patience for meetings like that.
Hardly a week goes by without another delay.
entries.русский: почти нисколько, почти никаких — обиходная разговорная замена few и little
entries.position: hardly modifies the central determiner any, which fills the central slot
entries.register: neutral — the everyday American default
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (hardly any people) and uncountable nouns (hardly any money). Never a singular countable noun (✗ hardly any chair), except in the separate frame hardly a + singular noun (hardly a day goes by).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — hardly any of the students, hardly any of it. No of before a bare noun: hardly any students.
entries.pattern: hardly any [plural countable / uncountable] · hardly any of [the/my/these + noun] · hardly any of [them/it] · hardly a [singular countable noun] · hardly any (pronoun)
entries.contrast: this is what Americans say instead of bare few and bare little in ordinary speech — hardly any time rather than little time, hardly any people rather than few people. It covers both countability types at once, which neither few nor little can do. It is negative-polarity, so the verb stays positive: ✓ There's hardly any left / ✗ There isn't hardly any left (negative concord — standard in several American dialects, nonstandard in writing; ✗ hardly no likewise). Distinguish hardly ever (frequency) and hardly alone (I could hardly hear you), which are adverbs, not determiners.
entries.variants: hardly any at all, hardly anything / hardly anyone (pronouns), hardly a, hardly ever, barely any, scarcely any
entries.see also: barely any, scarcely any, few, little, not many, next to no

entries.meaning: Names a quantity that is as close to zero as it can be without being zero.
examples: We had next to no warning before the layoffs.
There's next to no parking anywhere near the stadium.
The job offers next to no flexibility.
He bought the place for next to nothing in 2009.
Next to no one showed up to the hearing.
The study found next to no difference between the groups.
There were next to no seats left by the time we got there. (plural countable)
entries.русский: почти никакого — практически ноль
entries.position: central — next to modifies the central determiner no
entries.register: neutral to informal
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (next to no time, next to no warning) and plural countable nouns (next to no options, next to no results). Singular countable nouns are possible but awkward and rare (next to no chance works because chance is on the mass side of the line).
entries.with of: it does not take an of-phrase; the pronoun form is next to nothing (we got next to nothing out of them), and next to none covers the countable pronoun (next to none of them).
entries.pattern: next to no [uncountable / plural countable] · next to nothing (pronoun) · next to none of [them/the + plural] · for next to nothing (idiom: very cheaply)
entries.contrast: next to no is stronger than hardly any — it puts the quantity adjacent to zero rather than merely near it — and it is the emphatic sibling of little to no and virtually no. Where hardly any is negative-polarity and needs the verb positive, next to no is built on no and is already the negation, so the same rule applies: ✓ We had next to no warning, ✗ We didn't have next to no warning. The idiom for next to nothing means "very cheaply" and is fixed.
entries.variants: little to no, little or no, virtually no, practically no, almost no, next to nothing, next to none
entries.see also: hardly any, barely any, precious few / precious little, a shred of

entries.meaning: The ordinary conversational way of saying few — a small number, with the smallness stated as a denial of largeness.
examples: Not many people showed up for the first session.
Not many of the original crew are still with the company.
There are not many restaurants open this late.
Not many of them had ever flown before.
Not many companies can absorb a hit like that.
Q: How many applied? A: Not many.
entries.русский: немного, немногие — разг. замена few, с исчисляемыми
entries.position: not negates the central determiner many, which fills the central slot
entries.register: neutral, conversational
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — not many people, not many options. Never an uncountable noun (✗ not many time — use not much) and never a singular countable noun.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — not many of the applicants, not many of them. No of before a bare plural: not many applicants.
entries.pattern: not many [plural countable] · not many of [the/these + plural] · not many of [them] · not many (pronoun, standing alone) · there weren't many [plural] (negation on the verb instead)
entries.contrast: not many is the everyday spoken equivalent of bare few, and not much is the equivalent of bare little — the pair splits exactly on countability. Note where the negation sits: Not many people came negates inside the noun phrase, while There weren't many people moves it onto the verb, and the second is commoner in speech. As a pronoun not many stands alone (Not many did). It is the negated form of many, which lives in the large-quantity file.
entries.variants: not too many, not that many, not very many, there weren't many
entries.see also: not much, few, hardly any, many

entries.meaning: The ordinary conversational way of saying little — a small amount, stated as a denial of largeness.
examples: There's not much time before the store closes.
Not much of the report was still accurate.
Not much money was left in the fund by December.
He's not much of a cook, but he tries.
Not much has changed since the last audit.
There's not much point in arguing about it now.
entries.русский: немного, мало — разг. замена little, с неисчисляемыми
entries.position: not negates the central determiner much, which fills the central slot
entries.register: neutral, conversational
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — not much time, not much money. Never a plural countable noun (✗ not much people — use not many) and never a singular countable noun, except through the separate frame not much of a + singular noun (not much of a cook).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — not much of the report, not much of it. No of before a bare noun: not much time. The frame not much of a + singular countable noun is a distinct construction meaning "a poor example of" (not much of a view, not much of a plan).
entries.pattern: not much [uncountable] · not much of [the/my/this + noun] · not much of [it/that] · not much of a [singular countable noun] · there isn't much [uncountable] (negation on the verb instead)
entries.contrast: not much is the everyday spoken equivalent of bare little, and its countable partner is not many. Note where the negation goes: Not much time is left negates inside the noun phrase, There isn't much time left moves it to the verb, and speech prefers the second. The of a frame is a different thing entirely — not much of a swimmer is a judgment of quality, not of quantity. As a pronoun not much stands alone with no noun and takes a singular verb (Not much has changed). Do not stack a second negative on it: ✗ We didn't get not much sleep, ✗ We didn't get no sleep. That is negative concord, which is systematic and rule-governed in African American English, Southern American English, and other varieties, but is corrected in edited writing, where the single negative We didn't get much sleep is the form to write. It is the negated form of much, which lives in the large-quantity file.
entries.variants: not too much, not that much, not very much, not much of a, there isn't much
entries.see also: not many, little, less, hardly any, much

entries.meaning: Names a quantity that is small and ought not to be — the emphatic, aggrieved form of few and little.
examples: There are precious few jobs like that left in the county.
We have precious little evidence either way.
Precious few of the promises made it into the final bill.
The report offers precious little comfort to homeowners.
Precious few of them will still be in business next year.
She had precious little patience for that kind of question.
entries.русский: до обидного мало — эмфатическое, с ноткой возмущения
entries.position: central — precious intensifies the quantifier, which fills the central slot
entries.register: neutral to journalistic; rhetorical, faintly indignant
entries.goes with: precious few takes plural countable nouns only (precious few options); precious little takes uncountable nouns only (precious little evidence). The countability split is the same as for bare few and little, and crossing it is the same error: ✗ precious little options, ✗ precious few evidence.
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — precious few of the survivors, precious little of the money, precious little of it. No of before a bare noun.
entries.pattern: precious few [plural countable] · precious little [uncountable] · precious few of [the + plural] · precious little of [the/my + noun] · precious few / precious little (pronouns, standing alone)
entries.contrast: precious here is a pure intensifier meaning "distressingly," not the adjective meaning "valuable" — precious little sympathy is not sympathy that is precious. The pair intensifies the already-negative few and little, so it is more emphatic than hardly any and carries a note of complaint that hardly any does not. Because the base words are negative, no extra negation is needed or allowed: ✓ There is precious little evidence, ✗ There isn't precious little evidence.
entries.variants: precious few, precious little, very few, very little, damn few (coarse)
entries.see also: few, little, few if any, hardly any, next to no

entries.meaning: Names a quantity so small as to be nearly none — the formal register's version of hardly any.
examples: Scarcely any of the delegates had read the amendment.
There has been scarcely any rain since April.
Scarcely any trace of the settlement remains.
He had scarcely any formal training.
Scarcely any of it survived the move.
Scarcely a sound came from the next room.
entries.русский: едва ли сколько-нибудь — книжн. вариант hardly any
entries.position: scarcely modifies the central determiner any, which fills the central slot
entries.register: formal — the bookish member of the hardly / barely / scarcely trio
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (scarcely any visitors) and uncountable nouns (scarcely any rain). Never a singular countable noun, except in the separate frame scarcely a + singular noun (scarcely a sound).
entries.with of: of is required before another determiner or a pronoun — scarcely any of the delegates, scarcely any of it. No of before a bare noun.
entries.pattern: scarcely any [plural countable / uncountable] · scarcely any of [the/these + noun] · scarcely any of [them/it] · scarcely a [singular countable noun] · scarcely any (pronoun)
entries.contrast: identical in meaning to hardly any and barely any, and separated from them only by register — scarcely is the most formal and the least common in American speech. It is negative-polarity, so the verb stays positive: ✓ Scarcely any of them noticed, ✗ Scarcely none of them noticed. One inversion note: when scarcely is fronted as an adverb it triggers subject–auxiliary inversion (Scarcely had we sat down when the phone rang), but scarcely any inside a subject noun phrase does not — Scarcely any of them had read it keeps normal order.
entries.variants: hardly any, barely any, scarcely a, scarcely anything / scarcely anyone (pronouns), scarcely ever
entries.see also: hardly any, barely any, next to no, little

entries.meaning: Names the smallest amount there could be, in a frame that denies there was even that much.
examples: He didn't show the least bit of interest in the offer.
If she'd had the least bit of warning, she would have rescheduled.
There isn't the least bit of evidence for that claim.
We got through the whole week without the least bit of trouble.
Would it kill them to show the least bit of gratitude?
She wasn't the least bit surprised. (adverbial use, no of)
entries.pronunciation note: the keeps its weak pre-consonant form /ðə/, never /ði/; the of reduces to /ə/, giving thuh LEEST BIT uh
entries.русский: ни малейшей доли — в отрицании: «ни капельки не было»
entries.position: central — the whole phrase fills the central determiner slot
entries.register: neutral, conversational
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns — the least bit of trouble, the least bit of sense, the least bit of evidence, the least bit of privacy. Never a plural countable noun (✗ the least bit of options) and never a singular countable noun. Note that the least bit without of is an adverb of degree and is far commoner: not the least bit sorry, not the least bit surprised.
entries.with of: required when a noun follows — ✗ the least bit trouble. Drop the of and the phrase becomes the adverbial not the least bit + adjective, which is not a determiner at all.
entries.pattern: not the least bit of [uncountable noun] · without the least bit of [uncountable noun] · if [someone] had the least bit of [noun] · not the least bit [adjective] (adverb, not a determiner) · there isn't the least bit of [noun]
entries.contrast: the least bit of is negative-polarity: it lives under negation, in questions, and in if-clauses, and a plain affirmative ✗ We had the least bit of luck is not idiomatic. It is the colloquial cousin of a shred of and an iota of, and unlike either of them it happily takes homely nouns of comfort and convenience (the least bit of shade, the least bit of warning). Do not confuse it with least alone, which is an ordinary superlative needing no negation (the plan that causes the least disruption), or with the fixed adverbial not in the least, which modifies nothing.
entries.variants: not the least bit of, not the least bit (adverb), not in the least, the slightest bit of, a shred of, an ounce of
entries.see also: a shred of, an iota of, least, a bit of, hardly any

entries.meaning: Describes a quantity so small that the law or the rule declines to take notice of it — a legal threshold wearing the clothes of a measurement.
examples: The court held that three minutes of unpaid setup time was de minimis.
The employer treats occasional personal use of the copier as a de minimis fringe benefit.
Concentrations at that level are de minimis under the current standard.
The sampled clip ran too long to be de minimis use.
Counsel argued that the error was de minimis and could not have affected the verdict.
The rule includes a de minimis exception for shipments under $800.
entries.pronunciation note: both are current in American courtrooms and neither is corrected; the stress falls on MIN
entries.русский: юр.: ничтожно малый — такой, которым закон пренебрегает
entries.position: attributive. It stands where a determiner would (de minimis risk), but it can also follow one — a de minimis amount, the de minimis exception, this de minimis error — which is the proof that it is an adjective. It is also used predicatively: the harm was de minimis.
entries.register: legal and technical only. It is the head of the maxim de minimis non curat lex, "the law does not concern itself with trifles." An American meets it in tax rules (the de minimis fringe benefit, the de minimis safe harbor), in wage-and-hour and employment cases, in copyright and environmental law, and in the compliance memos that quote them. It is never neutral English, and outside that world it reads as showing off.
entries.type: Latin adjective phrase with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (de minimis risk, de minimis harm, de minimis use) and plural countable nouns (de minimis amounts, de minimis quantities, de minimis errors). With a singular countable noun it needs an article, exactly as an adjective does: a de minimis amount, never ✗ de minimis amount.
entries.with of: Not used — the phrase takes no of-phrase of its own. The partitive work is done by the noun it modifies: a de minimis amount of lead, a de minimis quantity of the compound.
entries.pattern: de minimis [uncountable / plural countable] · [a/the] de minimis [singular countable noun] · the de minimis exception/threshold/rule · [noun] is de minimis (predicative) · de minimis non curat lex (the full maxim)
entries.contrast: de minimis does not merely mean "very small." It means small enough that the law will disregard it, which is a conclusion rather than a measurement — a court calling an exposure de minimis is declining to act on it. That is the whole distance between de minimis harm and minimal harm: the second is a quantity, the first is a ruling. Against minimal, which is technical but ordinary English, de minimis is a term of art with a doctrine behind it. Against a scintilla of, the other Latin small of American law, note the grammar: de minimis modifies a noun, while a scintilla of takes one.
entries.variants: de minimis non curat lex (the full maxim), the de minimis rule, the de minimis exception, the de minimis threshold, minimal, negligible
entries.see also: minimal, a scintilla of, scant, slight, a modicum of

entries.meaning: Describes a quantity reduced to the smallest workable amount — small by design or by measurement rather than by disappointment.
examples: The upgrade required minimal effort from the users.
There was minimal damage to the roof.
We made minimal changes to the original draft.
The treatment has minimal side effects.
She charged us a minimal fee for the consultation.
The disruption was minimal, all things considered.
entries.русский: минимальный — сведённый к наименьшему рабочему количеству, намеренно
entries.position: it stands where a determiner would, but it can also follow one (the minimal disruption we caused), which proves it is an adjective
entries.register: neutral, leaning technical and corporate
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (minimal effort, minimal risk, minimal damage) and plural countable nouns (minimal changes, minimal side effects). With a singular countable noun it needs an article, exactly as an adjective does: a minimal fee, not ✗ minimal fee.
entries.with of: Not used — this word takes no of-phrase. The nominal a minimum of does that work instead: a minimum of three days.
entries.pattern: minimal [uncountable / plural countable] · [the/a] minimal [noun] · fairly/relatively/absolutely minimal · [noun] is minimal (predicative)
entries.contrast: minimal is an adjective, so unlike the quantifiers above it can be modified by a degree adverb, used predicatively, and preceded by a determiner. Strictly it is an absolute — from Latin minimus, "the smallest possible" — so fairly minimal and more minimal are logically loose, though both are ordinary in American usage and only style guides object. Against the determiner little, it is more clinical and less negative: minimal damage is a measurement, little damage is a judgment.
entries.variants: minimally (adverb), the bare minimum, a minimum of, negligible, nominal
entries.see also: scant, slight, sparse, a modicum of, little

entries.meaning: Describes a quantity that falls short of what is needed or expected — the formal register's version of bare little, and one of the few quantifying words that takes countable and uncountable nouns alike.
examples: There is scant evidence that the program worked.
The report paid scant attention to what any of it would cost.
That is scant comfort to the families still waiting for answers.
They did the whole job with scant resources and no permanent staff. (plural countable)
He has shown scant regard for the deadline since the day he took over.
Add a scant teaspoon of baking soda, not a heaping one. (singular — "barely a full")
entries.русский: скудный, едва достаточный — книжн.; сочетается и с исчисляемыми, и с неисчисляемыми
entries.position: attributive. It stands where a determiner would (scant evidence), but it can also follow one — the scant evidence we have, his scant regard for the rules — which is the proof that it is an adjective and not a central determiner. Unlike minimal and sparse it resists the predicative slot: The evidence is scant occurs but sounds stiff next to The evidence is thin.
entries.register: formal to journalistic
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (scant evidence, scant attention, scant comfort, scant regard) and plural countable nouns (scant resources, scant details). With a singular countable noun it needs an article, exactly as an adjective does, and it shifts meaning to "barely a full one": a scant teaspoon, a scant hour, a scant two miles. Never ✗ scant teaspoon with no article.
entries.with of: Not used — this word takes no of-phrase.
entries.pattern: scant [uncountable / plural countable] · [the/his/their] scant [noun] · a scant [singular unit noun] ("barely a full") · pay scant attention to [X] · show scant regard for [X]
entries.contrast: scant is the formal written cousin of bare little, and the test that separates them is position: little cannot follow a determiner, scant can — ✓ the scant evidence, ✗ the little evidence in that same sense. It carries the same disappointment bare little does (scant comfort means no real comfort at all), and it covers both countability types, which neither little nor few can do alone. Against minimal, which is neutral and technical, scant is a complaint; against sparse, which measures how thinly a quantity is spread, scant measures only how little of it there is. In a scant teaspoon it means "just short of," the exact opposite of a generous teaspoon. Keep it apart from scanty, which describes clothing and coverage rather than quantity.
entries.variants: scanty, scantily (adverb), a scant (+ unit noun), scant regard, scant attention, scant comfort
entries.see also: minimal, slight, sparse, little, precious few / precious little

entries.meaning: Describes a small degree or extent of something — faint, mild, or barely appreciable.
examples: There's been a slight delay with the connecting flight.
She has a slight accent that's hard to place.
We saw slight improvement after the second week.
There's a slight chance of snow tonight.
He hasn't the slightest idea what he's agreeing to.
The difference between the two samples was slight.
There were slight variations between the two batches. (plural countable — possible, but uncommon)
entries.русский: незначительный, лёгкий — малая степень или мера чего-либо
entries.position: attributive after a determiner (a slight delay, the slightest chance) or predicative (the difference was slight)
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns without an article (slight improvement, slight discomfort) and singular countable nouns with an article (a slight delay, a slight chance). With plural countable nouns it is possible but uncommon (slight variations). Because it is an adjective, it cannot replace the article the way a determiner can: ✗ slight delay held us up → ✓ a slight delay held us up.
entries.with of: Not used — this word takes no of-phrase.
entries.pattern: a slight [singular countable noun] · slight [uncountable noun] · the slightest [noun] · not the slightest [noun] · [noun] is slight (predicative)
entries.contrast: slight measures degree or intensity, not bulk — a slight delay is short, a slight accent is faint, a slight chance is improbable. That is what separates it from minimal, which measures quantity, and from little, which is a determiner and takes no article. Its superlative slightest is a negative-polarity favorite: not the slightest interest, without the slightest hesitation, hasn't the slightest idea. Keep it apart from the unrelated noun and verb slight meaning "an insult" / "to snub."
entries.variants: slightly (adverb), slighter, the slightest, not the slightest, the merest
entries.see also: minimal, scant, sparse, a hint of, a shade of, a little

entries.meaning: Describes something small in quantity and thinly distributed over an area or a set. --- ← The grammar of determiners · All categories · Quantifiers of large quantity
examples: The vegetation gets sparse above the tree line.
Attendance was sparse for a Tuesday matinee.
Data on the early years is sparse and unreliable.
He ran a hand through his sparse hair.
Sparse crowds gathered along the parade route.
The northern counties are sparsely populated.
entries.русский: редкий, разреженный — малочисленный и разбросанный по площади
entries.position: attributive (sparse vegetation, the sparse crowd) or predicative (the data are sparse)
entries.register: neutral, leaning descriptive and technical
entries.type: adjective with quantifying force — not a true determiner
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (sparse vegetation, sparse data, sparse attendance) and plural countable nouns (sparse crowds, sparse trees). With a singular countable noun it needs an article: a sparse crowd.
entries.with of: Not used — this word takes no of-phrase.
entries.pattern: sparse [uncountable / plural countable] · [a/the] sparse [noun] · sparsely populated (adverb) · [noun] is sparse (predicative) · sparser / more sparse
entries.contrast: sparse adds distribution to smallness: the quantity is small and thinly spread over an area, which is why it fits vegetation, hair, population, attendance, and data points, and why it sounds wrong for a compact quantity (sparse money is odd). Among the adjectives here, minimal measures amount, slight measures degree, and sparse measures density. Its nearest determiner-side relative is a smattering of, which does the same scattering work as a partitive phrase. The opposite is dense.
entries.variants: sparsely (adverb), sparser, sparsity / sparseness, thin, scattered
entries.see also: minimal, scant, slight, a smattering of, a trickle of
